title: F$^2$Agent: Financial Fusion of Agentic Intelligence for Multimodal Trading
summary: With increasingly diverse and heterogeneous information sources, effectively leveraging multimodal data is becoming pivotal for high-quality financial trading. Although recent advancements in Large Language Model (LLM)-based agents have enabled the ingestion of multimodal inputs, existing methods fail to capture nuanced cross-modal dependencies and remain vulnerable to market noise, due to limited multimodal modeling, ineffective fusion mechanisms, and inadequate robustness. To address these challenges, we propose F$^2$Agent, a novel multimodal agentic paradigm driven by the Financial Fusion of Agentic Intelligence. F$^2$Agent first deploys a hierarchy of specialized agents to comprehensively extract modality-specific signals. It further introduces a modality-aware adaptive fusion mechanism coupled with noise-robust consistency regularization to dynamically capture fine-grained inter-modality dependencies and generate noise-resilient trading signals. Extensive experiments on six stocks and cryptocurrency assets demonstrate that F$^2$Agent consistently outperforms 16 competitive baselines across multiple trading metrics, with over 20% relative improvement in annualized return on average. Notably, F$^2$Agent delivers returns of 120.48% on GOOG and 148.41% on TSLA, demonstrating its efficacy and robustness in varying market dynamics.

AI.tldr: F²Agent is a multimodal agentic paradigm that uses specialized agents for financial data extraction and modality-aware fusion with noise-robust consistency regularization to generate superior trading signals.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based agents for financial trading fail to capture nuanced cross-modal dependencies and remain vulnerable to market noise due to limited multimodal modeling, ineffective fusion mechanisms, and inadequate robustness.
AI.method: F²Agent deploys a hierarchy of specialized agents to extract modality-specific signals, then uses modality-aware adaptive fusion coupled with noise-robust consistency regularization to dynamically capture fine-grained inter-modality dependencies and generate noise-resilient trading signals.
AI.result: F²Agent consistently outperforms 16 competitive baselines across multiple trading metrics with over 20% relative improvement in annualized return on average, achieving returns of 120.48% on GOOG and 148.41% on TSLA.
AI.conclusion: F²Agent demonstrates efficacy and robustness in varying market dynamics by effectively leveraging multimodal data through financial fusion of agentic intelligence.

title: A Two-Tier Perspective on Inference-Time Parallelism in Multi-Agent LLM Systems
summary: Large language model (LLM)-driven multi-agent systems typically require multiple model invocations and complex coordination during inference, and their execution strategies directly affect system accuracy, latency, and computational cost. Parallel execution provides a means to improve inference-time efficiency. From the perspective of inference-time execution, this paper models parallelism in multi-agent systems as two distinct levels of decision processes: Replica Parallelism, which explores multiple complete solution paths at the task level, and Structural Parallelism, which enables concurrent execution within a single solution path through task decomposition. However, the roles of different forms of parallelism and their interrelationships still lack systematic study in terms of unified organization and coordination. We therefore propose TIPEX, a controllable execution framework that unifies these two levels of parallelism and coordinates their roles within the inference process under a unified execution semantics while supporting systematic combinations and analyses of different parallel strategies and parameter configurations. Systematic experiments on the GAIA benchmark demonstrate that inference-time parallelism can significantly improve accuracy and reduce end-to-end latency at the cost of increased token consumption. Further analysis shows that Replica and Structural Parallelism exhibit complementary effects across task complexities, with tasks of intermediate difficulty benefiting most from their coordination, while overly aggressive parallel strategies do not necessarily yield better performance.

AI.tldr: TIPEX is a controllable execution framework that unifies two levels of parallelism (Replica and Structural) in LLM-driven multi-agent systems to improve inference efficiency through coordinated parallel execution.
AI.motivation: LLM-driven multi-agent systems have complex coordination requirements during inference, with execution strategies directly affecting accuracy, latency, and computational cost. Existing approaches lack systematic study of different parallelism forms and their interrelationships, particularly regarding unified organization and coordination.
AI.method: The paper models parallelism at two levels: Replica Parallelism (exploring multiple complete solution paths at task level) and Structural Parallelism (enabling concurrent execution within single solution paths through task decomposition). TIPEX is proposed as a framework that unifies these two parallelism levels under unified execution semantics while supporting systematic combinations and analyses of different parallel strategies.
AI.result: Experiments on GAIA benchmark show inference-time parallelism significantly improves accuracy and reduces end-to-end latency, though at the cost of increased token consumption. Replica and Structural Parallelism exhibit complementary effects across task complexities, with intermediate-difficulty tasks benefiting most from coordination. Overly aggressive parallel strategies don't necessarily yield better performance.
AI.conclusion: TIPEX provides a systematic approach to coordinate Replica and Structural Parallelism in multi-agent systems, demonstrating that controlled parallel execution can optimize the accuracy-latency-computation trade-off, with different parallelism strategies showing complementary benefits based on task complexity.

title: Certifying Collective Reasoning in Multi-Agent Systems via Koopman Spectral Analysis
summary: Orchestrated collectives of large language model (LLM) agents that debate and vote are an emerging form of computational intelligence: the intelligent behaviour resides in the \emph{interaction}, not in any single agent. They improve task accuracy, yet remain black boxes at the system level: there is no principled test of convergence, no bound on the rounds needed, and no faithful account of what drove a decision. This paper develops a novel framework based on Koopman operator theory and validates its theoretical guarantees on multi-agent consensus dynamics. Treating the collective as one nonlinear dynamical system on a communication graph, we read its essential behaviour off the spectrum of its Koopman transfer operator, an exact linear representation of the nonlinear dynamics estimated from interaction traces. The spectrum yields three machine-checkable certificates: the sub-dominant eigenvalue $λ_2$ fixes the intrinsic timescale of reasoning and yields a convergence deadline computable \emph{before} the debate runs; its eigenvector names the coherent factions the collective reasons in, and $|λ_2|$ certifies when that explanation is valid; and the leading spectral coordinates form a compressed, auditable message basis. On an attention-consensus model, the deadline tracks observed convergence with log--log correlation $0.93$ and bounds it in 96\% of 24 configurations; attribution is exact whenever the spectrum certifies metastability; eight of 32 coordinates preserve the decision at 99.7\% fidelity; and a certificate learned from 15 debates held on 60/60 held-out debates. The study runs in minutes on a CPU, making spectral certification a practical layer for trustworthy collective reasoning.

AI.tldr: Spectral certification framework using Koopman operator theory provides machine-checkable guarantees for convergence, timing, and faction analysis in LLM collectives, making collective reasoning more transparent and trustworthy.
AI.motivation: LLM agent collectives that debate and vote improve task accuracy but remain black boxes at the system level—there's no principled test of convergence, no bound on reasoning rounds needed, and no faithful account of what drove decisions.
AI.method: Treats the collective as one nonlinear dynamical system on a communication graph and uses Koopman operator theory to extract essential behavior from interaction traces. The Koopman transfer operator provides an exact linear representation of the nonlinear dynamics, with its spectrum yielding three machine-checkable certificates.
AI.result: The framework achieves: 1) convergence deadline tracking with log-log correlation 0.93, bounding convergence in 96% of configurations; 2) exact attribution when spectrum certifies metastability; 3) eight of 32 coordinates preserve decisions at 99.7% fidelity; and 4) certificates learned from 15 debates generalize to 60/60 held-out debates. The system runs in minutes on a CPU.
AI.conclusion: Spectral certification provides a practical layer for trustworthy collective reasoning by offering theoretical guarantees on convergence timing, faction identification, and explanation validity, making LLM agent collectives less of a black box while maintaining computational efficiency.

title: ASGE-RR: Agentic Service Graph Embedding with Revisable Reservations for Dynamic AI-Agent Calls
summary:
AI-agent workflows often involve remote calls to models, memory stores, and tools distributed across a network. As execution progresses, these dependency calls collectively form an agentic service graph (ASG). Unlike traditional service requests, many dependency calls are revealed only at runtime. Consequently, allocating resources to a currently visible call may consume capacity later needed by a call from a higher-value workflow. We formulate this challenge as Agentic Service Graph Embedding (ASGE), an online network-control problem that maps runtime-revealed workflow calls to service replicas and network paths under capacity, cost and deadline constraints. We present ASGE-RR, an online ASGE controller with revisable reservations. ASGE-RR protects capacity for likely future calls while enforcing the constraints. ASGE-RR evaluates candidate replica-and-path mappings against predicted workflow continuations and updates reservations as new execution information becomes available.
  We evaluate ASGE-RR using OpenHands and GPT Researcher workflows executed with gpt-5.6-luna and replayed over in two complementary experimental environments, a controlled Docker testbed and a WAN testbed. The investigation shows that all the evaluated AI-agent tasks expose at least one runtime-revealed dependency call that can be steered before connection establishment. Exploiting this control point, even though the experimental environments are small-scale, ASGE-RR already demonstrates noticeable potential: It completes (up to) 10% more workflow value than a same-information rolling-horizon controller and a current-call steering controller on the WAN testbed. The results suggest that runtime-revealed workflow structure creates a new network control opportunity: protecting resources for likely future calls allows more AI-agent workflows to finish in time.

AI.tldr: ASGE-RR is an online controller that protects network capacity for runtime-revealed AI-agent workflow calls, improving workflow completion rates by up to 10% compared to existing approaches.
AI.motivation: AI-agent workflows have runtime-revealed dependency calls that form agentic service graphs (ASGs). Traditional resource allocation fails because allocating to current visible calls may consume capacity needed later by higher-value workflow calls.
AI.method: ASGE-RR uses revisable reservations to protect capacity for likely future calls while enforcing constraints. It evaluates candidate replica-and-path mappings against predicted workflow continuations and updates reservations as new execution information becomes available.
AI.result: All evaluated AI-agent tasks exposed at least one runtime-revealed dependency call that could be steered. ASGE-RR completed up to 10% more workflow value than rolling-horizon and current-call steering controllers on WAN testbeds.
AI.conclusion: Runtime-revealed workflow structure creates a new network control opportunity where protecting resources for likely future calls allows more AI-agent workflows to finish in time, demonstrating noticeable potential even in small-scale environments.

title: MS-MLB: An Open Machine Learning Benchmark for Blood-Based MS Classification
summary: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is diagnosed through clinical assessment, magnetic resonance imaging, laboratory evidence when appropriate, and exclusion of better explanations. Blood RNA expression data may contain disease associated immune signal, but a blood RNA classifier cannot be treated as a replacement for clinical diagnosis. This paper presents MS-MLB (Multiple Sclerosis Machine Learning Benchmark), a reproducible open benchmark for machine learning based MS research classification from whole blood RNA expression data. MS-MLB uses the public GSE17048 cohort, converts it into an MS versus healthy control task, and evaluates multiple algorithms under a shared, leakage controlled pipeline that a researcher can rerun without reconfiguring the evaluation. The evaluation includes nested cross-validation, an untouched stratified holdout set, bootstrap confidence intervals, ROC and precision recall analysis, calibration measurement, and an exploratory MS Research Score. In the final benchmark summary, Gradient Boosting ranked first by MS Research Score on the holdout set, with an MS Research Score of 93.83, AUC-ROC of 0.989, sensitivity of 0.950, specificity of 0.778, $F_{1}$ score of 0.927, and Brier score of 0.050. Prior studies have applied machine learning to MS blood transcriptomic data, including PBMC stage classification and whole blood diagnostic signature modeling. The contribution here is different and narrower. To our knowledge, MS-MLB is the first open benchmark focused on MS versus healthy control classification from GSE17048 whole blood RNA expression data with a documented external model submission pathway built into the framework. The score is intended for research comparison only and has not been clinically validated. The benchmark is accessible here: https://github.com/duckyquang/MS-MLB.

AI.tldr: MS-MLB is an open, reproducible machine learning benchmark for multiple sclerosis vs. healthy control classification using whole blood RNA expression data from the GSE17048 cohort.
AI.motivation: While blood RNA expression data contains disease-associated immune signals, a blood RNA classifier cannot replace clinical diagnosis. There's a need for standardized, reproducible benchmarks in MS machine learning research to ensure fair comparison and prevent data leakage.
AI.method: The benchmark uses GSE17048 cohort data converted to MS vs. healthy control classification task. It implements a shared, leakage-controlled pipeline with nested cross-validation, untouched stratified holdout set, bootstrap confidence intervals, ROC/precision-recall analysis, calibration measurement, and an exploratory MS Research Score. The framework allows external model submissions.
AI.result: Gradient Boosting performed best with MS Research Score of 93.83, AUC-ROC of 0.989, sensitivity of 0.950, specificity of 0.778, F₁ score of 0.927, and Brier score of 0.050 on the holdout set.
AI.conclusion: MS-MLB provides the first open benchmark for MS vs. healthy control classification from GSE17048 whole blood RNA data with an external model submission pathway. The benchmark is intended for research comparison only and not clinically validated, but offers a standardized framework for reproducible machine learning research in MS.

title: Agentic Nesting: A New Methodology for Existing Enterprise Application Integration and Services
summary: Enterprise operations extensively rely on multiple heterogeneous business systems and information applications, which also result in severe data silos and process fragmentation. Enterprises have invested considerable financial and material resources in building these applications, however, effectively leveraging and orchestrating them remains a formidable challenge. Conventional approaches to enterprise application integration, encompassing middleware architectures such as Enterprise Service Bus (ESB), API gateway infrastructures, and Robotic Process Automation (RPA), suffer from inherent limitations like high architectural coupling, escalating operation and maintenance costs, and limited intelligence capabilities. This paper proposes Agentic Nesting, a multi-agent collaboration framework in which existing enterprise applications are encapsulated as autonomous AI agents within a hierarchically nested structure. Rather than flat interconnection, agents are organized into layered stewardship topologies that mirror the compositional complexity of enterprise ecosystems. The framework extracts a digital agent proxy from each legacy application to enable natural-language interaction and autonomous manipulation, coordinates multiple agents through a central orchestrator for task decomposition and dynamic dispatching, and exposes a unified conversational interface for cross-application querying and process orchestration. The main contributions of this paper are the proposition of the "Application-as-Agent" integration paradigm and the "Conversation-as-Integration" interaction philosophy, together with an exploration of the generalization potential of this methodology in scenarios encompassing heterogeneous system coordination, and large-scale data applications.

AI.tldr: Agentic Nesting proposes a multi-agent framework where enterprise applications are encapsulated as AI agents in hierarchical structures, enabling natural-language interaction and autonomous coordination through a central orchestrator.
AI.motivation: Enterprises face challenges with data silos and process fragmentation due to multiple heterogeneous systems. Traditional integration methods (ESB, API gateways, RPA) have limitations including high architectural coupling, high operational costs, and limited intelligence capabilities.
AI.method: The framework extracts digital agent proxies from legacy applications for natural-language interaction, organizes agents into hierarchical stewardship topologies that mirror enterprise complexity, uses a central orchestrator for task decomposition and dynamic dispatching, and provides unified conversational interfaces for cross-application coordination.
AI.result: The paper introduces the "Application-as-Agent" integration paradigm and "Conversation-as-Integration" interaction philosophy, demonstrating their potential for heterogeneous system coordination and large-scale data applications.
AI.conclusion: Agentic Nesting offers a novel approach to enterprise integration by transforming legacy applications into intelligent agents within hierarchical structures, addressing limitations of traditional methods while enabling more natural and intelligent cross-application coordination.

title: DoctorAgents: an agentic framework to iteratively refine AutoML pipeline for small clinical temporal data
summary: Clinical machine learning (ML) has the potential to support high-stakes medical decision-making, but reliable deployment is often constrained by scarce, heterogeneous, and temporal complexity. Developing effective ML pipelines for such data remains time-consuming and error-prone, while existing automated machine learning (AutoML) systems only partially address this challenge because they largely rely on brute-force search over predefined spaces and lack explicit reasoning and memory. We therefore reformulate AutoML for small clinical data from exhaustive search to reasoning-driven refinement. We propose DoctorAgents, an agentic AI framework that autonomously constructs and optimizes end-to-end ML pipelines through specialized large language model (LLM) agents for generation, validation, and refinement. DoctorAgents backpropagates natural-language feedback through textual gradient descent to perform targeted updates without exhaustive search. Experiments across diverse clinical tasks show that DoctorAgents consistently outperforms established AutoML baselines while producing more interpretable task-specific representations.

AI.tldr: DoctorAgents is an agentic AI framework that uses specialized LLM agents to autonomously build and optimize clinical ML pipelines through reasoning-driven refinement rather than brute-force search, outperforming traditional AutoML methods.
AI.motivation: Clinical ML faces challenges with scarce, heterogeneous, and temporally complex data, making reliable deployment difficult. Existing AutoML systems rely on brute-force search over predefined spaces and lack explicit reasoning and memory, making them insufficient for clinical data challenges.
AI.method: DoctorAgents reformulates AutoML for clinical data from exhaustive search to reasoning-driven refinement using specialized LLM agents for generation, validation, and refinement. It employs textual gradient descent to backpropagate natural-language feedback for targeted updates without exhaustive search.
AI.result: Experiments across diverse clinical tasks show DoctorAgents consistently outperforms established AutoML baselines while producing more interpretable task-specific representations.
AI.conclusion: The agentic AI framework successfully addresses limitations of traditional AutoML for clinical data by using reasoning-driven refinement rather than brute-force search, enabling more effective and interpretable clinical ML pipeline development.

title: When Do Corrective Features Help? An Agent for Corrective Feature Discovery on Black-Box Forecasters
summary: Frozen pretrained forecasters often fail in structured, recurring ways that are costly to repair through fine-tuning. We study corrective feature discovery: mining interpretable features of a frozen forecaster's residual to drive a lightweight post-hoc corrector. Prior automated feature engineering models the data-generating process; corrective features instead model the model-failure process. We present CRAFTER (Corrective Residual Agent with Feature-based Temporal Exploration and Reasoning), which keeps the backbone frozen and mines its residual with two complementary generators: a compositional search over the raw input channels, and a large language model (LLM) that proposes named feature combinations, binary flags, and short executable code. A single validation-grounded gate accepts or rejects every candidate regardless of its origin, and a validation-selected corrector applies the accepted features or leaves the forecast unchanged. This source-agnostic pipeline also allows prior feature-engineering systems to be evaluated under identical conditions, making CRAFTER an instrument for attributing forecast improvements to the feature source alone. Across six public datasets and six frozen backbones, CRAFTER surpasses every dedicated feature-engineering system at every feature budget, roughly doubling the improvement achieved by the corrector alone and reducing the error of the weakest backbones by up to 27%. These gains are robust across different LLM backends and persist even when applied on top of fine-tuned backbones.

AI.tldr: CRAFTER is a corrective feature discovery system that mines interpretable features from frozen forecasters' residuals to drive lightweight post-hoc correctors, outperforming dedicated feature-engineering systems and significantly reducing forecasting errors.
AI.motivation: Frozen pretrained forecasters often fail in structured, recurring ways that are costly to repair through fine-tuning. The paper aims to develop a method for corrective feature discovery that models the model-failure process rather than the data-generating process, enabling lightweight correction of frozen forecasters.
AI.method: CRAFTER keeps the backbone frozen and mines its residuals using two complementary generators: 1) compositional search over raw input channels, and 2) LLM-based proposals for named feature combinations, binary flags, and short executable code. A validation-grounded gate accepts/rejects candidates, and a validation-selected corrector applies accepted features or leaves forecasts unchanged.
AI.result: Across six public datasets and six frozen backbones, CRAFTER surpasses every dedicated feature-engineering system at every feature budget, roughly doubling the improvement achieved by the corrector alone and reducing the error of the weakest backbones by up to 27%. Gains are robust across different LLM backends and persist even when applied on top of fine-tuned backbones.
AI.conclusion: CRAFTER provides an effective framework for corrective feature discovery that significantly improves frozen forecasters' performance through interpretable residual-based corrections, while also serving as an instrument for attributing forecast improvements to feature sources under identical conditions.

title: The Ignition Index: Measuring Global Workspace Dynamics in Language Models
summary: We introduce the Ignition Index (I), a validated scalar metric that operationalizes Global Workspace Theory's (GWT) all-or-none ignition prediction in transformer language models. The metric fits a four-parameter sigmoid to per-layer linear probe accuracy as a function of input signal strength, extracting steepness parameter beta-hat: high values indicate abrupt, ignition-like transitions; low values indicate graded build-up. Across 11 models spanning five architecture families, shuffled-label controls demonstrate 9.6-fold selectivity for genuine linguistic structure over spurious probe capacity (p < 0.001, Mann-Whitney U-test). We find: (1) Feedforward transformers exceed SSMs by 89% in aggregate beta-hat (p < 1e-13, Cohen's d = 0.52), with Mamba exhibiting near-linear profiles consistent with absent global broadcast. (2) Huginn-3.5B exhibits 2.12-fold higher ignition along its iteration axis than its depth axis, demonstrating that recurrent architectures manifest workspace-like transitions along the recurrence dimension. (3) Pythia-410M shows a PELT-detected phase transition at training step 256 (+67%), preceding induction-head formation. (4) Hypotheses linking ignition to model scale and signal strength were not confirmed, suggesting transformer architectures may saturate available ignition mechanisms. The Ignition Index provides the first validated quantitative bridge between GWT's dynamical predictions and mechanistic interpretability, with 9.6-fold measurement selectivity and architecture-level discriminability not previously characterized in the scaling literature. Code: https://github.com/saman-rahbar/ignition-index

AI.tldr: The Ignition Index (I) is a new metric that quantifies Global Workspace Theory's ignition prediction in transformer models, measuring how abruptly information processing transitions from local to global activation across layers.
AI.motivation: To bridge Global Workspace Theory's conceptual predictions about conscious access with mechanistic interpretability of language models, creating a validated quantitative measure of "ignition" (all-or-none global activation) in neural networks.
AI.method: Fit four-parameter sigmoid to per-layer linear probe accuracy as function of input signal strength, extracting steepness parameter beta-hat. Applied across 11 models from 5 architecture families with shuffled-label controls to distinguish genuine linguistic structure from spurious probe capacity.
AI.result: Found 9.6-fold selectivity for linguistic structure; feedforward transformers exceed SSMs by 89% in ignition; Huginn shows ignition along recurrence dimension; Pythia shows phase transition at step 256 preceding induction-head formation; no link found between ignition and model scale/signal strength.
AI.conclusion: The Ignition Index provides first validated quantitative bridge between GWT predictions and mechanistic interpretability, offering architecture-level discriminability not previously characterized, suggesting transformers may saturate available ignition mechanisms.

title: Adaptive Arena-based Contestable Argumentative Network-of-Experts for Open-Ended Care Plan Coordination
comment: Accepted at the 4th International Conference on Frontiers of Artificial Intelligence, Ethics, and Multidisciplinary Applications
summary: Care plan coordination demands synthesizing heterogeneous clinical, functional, and psychosocial information across multiple professional disciplines, where monolithic LLM pipelines cannot perform in a transparent or safe manner. We present CANOE (Contestable Argumentative Network-of-Experts), a multi-agent neuro-symbolic framework that addresses these limitations through five modules: complexity assessment, adaptive team recruitment, role-based argumentative computation via an Arena-based Quantitative Bipolar Argumentation Framework (A-QBAF), human-in-the-loop contestation, and care-plan synthesis. Role-specialized agents generate supporting and attacking arguments for candidate interventions; conflicts are resolved through arena-based clash resolution before acceptability scores propagate across the argumentation graph. Care planners may accept, reject, edit, or add arguments, and the framework will deterministically recompute the final plan. Evaluation on Discharge Me! and MedicalRAG using ROUGE-L, AlignScore, MEDCON F1, FKGL, and LLM-as-a-judge shows that medically fine-tuned models achieve the strongest clinical correctness and safety, while CANOE's argumentative structure provides faithful explanation and human contestability.

AI.tldr: CANOE is a multi-agent neuro-symbolic framework for care plan coordination that uses role-specialized agents to generate arguments for interventions, resolves conflicts through arena-based argumentation, and allows human contestation before synthesizing final care plans.
AI.motivation: Current monolithic LLM pipelines cannot handle care plan coordination transparently or safely, as it requires synthesizing heterogeneous clinical, functional, and psychosocial information across multiple professional disciplines.
AI.method: CANOE uses five modules: complexity assessment, adaptive team recruitment, role-based argumentative computation via A-QBAF (Arena-based Quantitative Bipolar Argumentation Framework), human-in-the-loop contestation, and care-plan synthesis. Role-specialized agents generate supporting/attacking arguments, conflicts are resolved through arena-based clash resolution, and acceptability scores propagate across the argumentation graph.
AI.result: Evaluation on Discharge Me! and MedicalRAG datasets shows medically fine-tuned models achieve strongest clinical correctness and safety, while CANOE's argumentative structure provides faithful explanation and human contestability. Metrics included ROUGE-L, AlignScore, MEDCON F1, FKGL, and LLM-as-a-judge.
AI.conclusion: CANOE addresses limitations of monolithic LLM approaches by providing a transparent, contestable framework for care plan coordination that combines medical domain expertise with argumentative reasoning and human oversight capabilities.

title: PPDL: LLM-Based Flows as Probabilistic Programs
summary: Building reliable applications that leverage large language models (LLMs) remains a significant challenge. While LLMs offer impressive capabilities across diverse tasks, their outputs often lack accuracy and provide no clear measure of confidence. This uncertainty compounds in flows of multiple calls to LLMs and other tools, making it difficult for developers and end-users to trust the results. This paper introduces a probabilistic language for programming LLM-based flows. It enables developers to quantify and propagate uncertainty throughout the application's flow, and experiment with different inference scaling techniques without adding a single line of code beyond the flow's logic. We present an experimental study to demonstrate this capability, and a case study building a theorem proving agent for the Rocq theorem prover.

AI.tldr: A probabilistic programming language that enables developers to quantify and propagate uncertainty in LLM-based applications, allowing experimentation with inference techniques without extra code.
AI.motivation: LLMs lack reliability measures and confidence scores, making it hard to trust results in complex multi-LLM flows. The uncertainty compounds across multiple calls, creating challenges for developers and end-users.
AI.method: Introduces a probabilistic programming language specifically designed for programming LLM-based flows. This language enables developers to quantify uncertainty throughout application flows and experiment with different inference scaling techniques without writing additional code beyond the core logic.
AI.result: The paper presents an experimental study demonstrating the language's capability, including a case study building a theorem proving agent for the Rocq theorem prover.
AI.conclusion: The probabilistic programming language successfully addresses the uncertainty problem in LLM-based applications by providing a framework to quantify and propagate confidence measures throughout complex flows.

title: Woodpecker Distillation: Weak Models Diagnose Reasoning Bugs in Strong Models
summary:
Large language models often fail on reasoning tasks despite possessing the capability to solve them. We argue that many such failures arise from localized reasoning bugs in intermediate steps rather than from global incompetence. We show that these bugs are frequently repairable: inserting a short patch generated by a weak probe model after the same strong-model reasoning prefix can redirect the trajectory toward a correct solution.
  However, this corrective effect is not reliably internalized by directly fine-tuning on weak patches or repaired trajectories, suggesting that the useful signal lies not in the intervention text itself, but in how it reshapes the model's future reasoning distribution. We therefore propose Woodpecker Distillation, a weak-to-strong training framework that learns from contrastive local interventions. Our method contrasts successful and unsuccessful weak-model patches at the same prefix, constructs a corrective teacher distribution from their induced future token predictions, and distills this signal into the strong model.
  Experiments on mathematical reasoning benchmarks show that Woodpecker Distillation consistently improves strong-model performance and outperforms direct imitation baselines.

AI.tldr: Woodpecker Distillation improves strong LLM reasoning by learning from contrastive weak-model patches rather than direct imitation, fixing localized reasoning bugs without requiring global retraining.
AI.motivation: Large language models often fail on reasoning tasks despite having the capability to solve them, with failures arising from localized reasoning bugs rather than global incompetence. These bugs are frequently repairable, but direct fine-tuning on weak patches doesn't reliably internalize the corrective effect.
AI.method: Propose Woodpecker Distillation, a weak-to-strong training framework that learns from contrastive local interventions. The method contrasts successful and unsuccessful weak-model patches at the same reasoning prefix, constructs a corrective teacher distribution from their induced future token predictions, and distills this signal into the strong model.
AI.result: Experiments on mathematical reasoning benchmarks show that Woodpecker Distillation consistently improves strong-model performance and outperforms direct imitation baselines.
AI.conclusion: The useful signal for fixing reasoning bugs lies not in the intervention text itself, but in how it reshapes the model's future reasoning distribution. Woodpecker Distillation provides an effective way to leverage weak models to improve strong ones by focusing on contrastive local interventions rather than direct imitation.

title: IFlowNets: Extending Generative Samplers to Learn Strategies in Incomplete Information Games
comment: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2025 Workshop on Dynamics at the Frontiers of Optimization, Sampling, and Games
summary: While many algorithms blend reinforcement learning (RL) with counterfactual regret (CFR) methods to leverage tradeoffs in computational speed and performance, there are fewer investigations into generative sampling frameworks in game theoretic applications in incomplete information games. We extend a generative flow network framework, Adversarial Flow Networks (AFlowNets), to incomplete information games, called Information Flow Networks (IFNs). We prove that previously established constraints for generative flow networks in complete information games are inadmissible for obtaining valid densities (corresponding to player strategies) and a valid training objective. We show that our proposed generalization, IFlowNets, alleviates this issue and strictly generalizes AFlowNets. In preliminary results for three standard game environments, IFlowNets perform comparably to or better than Outcome Sampling Monte Carlo Counterfactual Regret (OSMCCFR) and standard RL-based methods in performance and speed.

AI.tldr: Extends Adversarial Flow Networks to incomplete information games as Information Flow Networks, addressing limitations in generative sampling frameworks and showing competitive performance against existing methods.
AI.motivation: There are limited investigations into generative sampling frameworks for game theoretic applications in incomplete information games, despite many RL+CFR hybrid methods. Previous constraints for generative flow networks in complete information games don't work properly for incomplete information settings.
AI.method: Extends Adversarial Flow Networks (AFlowNets) to incomplete information games, creating Information Flow Networks (IFNs). Proves that previous constraints for generative flow networks are inadmissible for obtaining valid densities/strategies and valid training objectives. Proposes a generalization called IFlowNets that alleviates these issues.
AI.result: IFlowNets strictly generalize AFlowNets and work properly for incomplete information games. In preliminary experiments across three standard game environments, IFlowNets perform comparably to or better than Outcome Sampling Monte Carlo Counterfactual Regret (OSMCCFR) and standard RL-based methods in both performance and speed.
AI.conclusion: Information Flow Networks successfully extend generative flow network frameworks to incomplete information games, overcoming limitations of previous approaches and demonstrating competitive performance against state-of-the-art methods in both accuracy and computational efficiency.

title: Decoupling Perception from Description: Computation-Grounded Representation Alignment between Multivariate Time Series and Language
comment: 46 pages, 9 figures, including supplementary material. Submitted to AAAI 2027. Xinran Feng and Yi Xie contributed equally
summary: Training multimodal models to align time series with language runs into a self-supervision trap. The usual recipe asks an LLM to read a series and write a description, so label quality is capped by the perceptual skill the model is supposed to learn. The data can never teach more than the labeler already knows. A second gap makes this worse: most datasets use a single variable, but the patterns that matter (cross-channel correlation, lead-lag structure, co-occurring anomalies) appear only with several variables, right where the labeling LLM's limits are most exposed. These two problems create a trilemma: existing methods are reliable, realistic, or scalable, but none achieves all three. We resolve this by decoupling perception from description. Deterministic code computes a set of statistics from real, open-source multivariate series; the LLM verbalizes those precomputed facts. Perception, which LLMs do poorly, is handled by computation, while the LLM handles expression. This produces CGTime, our 4B-parameter computation-grounded time-series-language model. CGTime outperforms far larger general-purpose models on multivariate understanding tasks: it attains the best multivariate fact score on our held-out benchmark (0.283 vs. 0.173 for GPT-4o-mini and 0.203 for GPT-5.4-nano), a gap that survives Holm-corrected paired significance tests against every baseline. It also states verifiable numerical facts in generated captions more accurately and covers a broader range of statistical properties.

AI.tldr: CGTime is a 4B-parameter computation-grounded time-series-language model that decouples perception (handled by deterministic code) from description (handled by LLM), outperforming larger general-purpose models on multivariate time series understanding tasks.
AI.motivation: Current methods for training multimodal models to align time series with language face a "self-supervision trap" where label quality is limited by the perceptual skill the model is supposed to learn. Existing datasets typically use single variables, missing important multivariate patterns like cross-channel correlation, lead-lag structure, and co-occurring anomalies. This creates a trilemma where methods are either reliable, realistic, or scalable, but never all three.
AI.method: The approach decouples perception from description: deterministic code computes statistics from real, open-source multivariate time series, while an LLM verbalizes these precomputed facts. This computation-grounded approach handles perception (where LLMs are weak) through computation and expression (where LLMs excel) through language modeling.
AI.result: CGTime outperforms far larger general-purpose models on multivariate understanding tasks: achieves best multivariate fact score (0.283 vs. 0.173 for GPT-4o-mini, 0.203 for GPT-5.4-nano), with the gap surviving Holm-corrected significance tests. It also states verifiable numerical facts more accurately and covers broader statistical properties in generated captions.
AI.conclusion: By decoupling perception from description and grounding time series understanding in computed statistics rather than LLM-generated labels, the proposed computation-grounded approach breaks the self-supervision trap and achieves reliable, realistic, and scalable multivariate time series language understanding.

title: From Continuous Predictors to Clinical Thresholds: Early Evidence on Performance Trade-offs of Guideline-Based Categorisation for Ischaemic Stroke Outcome Prediction
summary: Machine learning models achieve strong predictive accuracy for 90-day outcome prediction in acute ischaemic stroke, yet clinical adoption is limited by the misalignment of model explanations with clinicians' reasoning. Motivated by a clinician user study calling for clinical guideline-aligned cut-offs, we ask whether continuous predictors can be replaced by clinically informed categorical encodings without sacrificing performance. On a multi-centre European registry stratified into three treatment cohorts, we compare standard and fully categorised gradient-boosted models, the latter using stroke guideline-aligned, treatment-specific thresholds. The fully categorised models are statistically indistinguishable from their continuous counterparts in two of the treatment cohorts, with a significant drop in predictive accuracy in one cohort. Global feature importance rankings remain consistent, suggesting that discretising continuous predictors into guideline-based categories preserves the core hierarchy of prognostic factors across all treatment groups. Guideline-based categorisation is thus a viable design choice for stroke-outcome models.

AI.tldr: Researchers show that using clinical guideline-aligned categorical cutoffs for continuous predictors in stroke outcome models preserves predictive performance while making models more clinically interpretable.
AI.motivation: Despite strong predictive accuracy of ML models for 90-day stroke outcome prediction, clinical adoption is limited because model explanations don't align with clinicians' reasoning. A user study revealed clinicians want guideline-aligned cutoffs for better interpretability.
AI.method: Compared standard gradient-boosted models with fully categorised versions using stroke guideline-aligned, treatment-specific thresholds on a multi-centre European registry. The study involved three treatment cohorts with stratification.
AI.result: Fully categorised models performed statistically similarly to continuous models in two treatment cohorts, with only one cohort showing significant performance drop. Global feature importance rankings remained consistent across all models, preserving prognostic factor hierarchy.
AI.conclusion: Discretising continuous predictors into guideline-based categories is a viable design choice for stroke outcome models, offering clinical interpretability without significant performance sacrifice.

title: Hybrid-Adaptive Thread Tuning to Mitigate Simulation Execution Bottlenecks in High-Performance Reinforcement Learning Inference
summary: In simulation-in-the-loop decision-making systems, reinforcement learning (RL) inference is often constrained by simulator-side execution overhead, where workloads are highly dynamic and sensitive to runtime thread configurations. Existing multithreaded strategies struggle to match thread resources before or during execution, causing resource contention, scheduling overhead, and reduced throughput. Through empirical analysis, we identify the ratio of task execution time to scheduling time as the key factor determining the optimal thread count. Building on this insight, we propose AutoThread, a hybrid adaptive thread-tuning method for mitigating simulation bottlenecks in RL inference. AutoThread employs a Physics-Informed Neural Operator (PINO) as a thread-count predictor and incorporates a finite-source M/M/1 queueing model to constrain and guide prediction, enabling fast and accurate estimation under dynamic workloads. It further performs load-aware online fine-tuning to compensate for prediction errors and refine resource allocation. Experiments show that AutoThread improves average speedup by 18.4\% over static strategies, achieves average throughput of 1.7x and 1.8x that of XGBoost and Reinforcer, respectively, and reduces execution time by up to 83.8\% compared with state-of-the-art methods. Our code and dataset are publicly available at https://github.com/suchenjm/AutoThread.

AI.tldr: AutoThread is a hybrid adaptive thread-tuning method that uses a Physics-Informed Neural Operator for thread prediction and queueing theory constraints to optimize simulation-in-the-loop RL inference by dynamically adjusting thread resources based on workload characteristics.
AI.motivation: In simulation-in-the-loop RL systems, simulator-side execution overhead creates bottlenecks due to highly dynamic workloads that are sensitive to thread configurations. Existing multithreading strategies struggle to properly match thread resources during execution, causing resource contention, scheduling overhead, and reduced throughput.
AI.method: AutoThread combines a Physics-Informed Neural Operator (PINO) as a thread-count predictor with a finite-source M/M/1 queueing model to constrain predictions. It performs empirical analysis to identify the task execution time to scheduling time ratio as the key factor for optimal thread count. The method includes load-aware online fine-tuning to compensate for prediction errors and refine resource allocation.
AI.result: AutoThread improves average speedup by 18.4% over static strategies, achieves average throughput of 1.7x and 1.8x compared to XGBoost and Reinforcer respectively, and reduces execution time by up to 83.8% compared to state-of-the-art methods.
AI.conclusion: AutoThread effectively addresses simulation bottlenecks in RL inference through adaptive thread-tuning that combines machine learning prediction with queueing theory constraints, significantly outperforming existing methods in dynamic workload scenarios.

title: Disentangling 3D Modeling from Spatial Reasoning
summary: In this work, we explore an alternative paradigm for spatial reasoning by explicitly disentangling 3D perception from reasoning, rather than jointly acquiring implicit 3D perception and reasoning through large-scale training. Our key observation is that modern perception models excel at estimating continuous 3D geometry, whereas large language models (LLMs) are particularly effective at compositional and symbolic reasoning. Motivated by these complementary strengths, we propose the Disentangled Spatial Reasoner (DiSR), a simple yet effective framework that reconstructs the physical world into structured 3D evidence using off-the-shelf expert perception models and fine-tunes an LLM with LoRA to perform reasoning solely over this explicit geometric evidence. Without large-scale 3D VQA training or complex tool-use policies, DiSR achieves competitive performance on popular spatial reasoning benchmarks. Beyond its strong performance, DiSR offers improved interpretability, modularity, and computational efficiency, demonstrating that explicit separation of perception and reasoning is a scalable and effective alternative paradigm to end-to-end modeling for spatial intelligence.

AI.tldr: A framework called DiSR that disentangles 3D perception from spatial reasoning by using expert perception models to extract explicit 3D geometric evidence, then fine-tuning LLMs to reason over this structured evidence, achieving competitive performance without large-scale 3D VQA training.
AI.motivation: Current approaches typically learn 3D perception and spatial reasoning jointly through large-scale training, but the authors observed that modern perception models excel at continuous 3D geometry estimation while LLMs are strong at compositional/symbolic reasoning. They want to leverage these complementary strengths separately rather than learning them implicitly together.
AI.method: DiSR uses off-the-shelf expert perception models to reconstruct the physical world into structured 3D evidence. It then fine-tunes a large language model with LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) to perform reasoning solely over this explicit geometric evidence. The framework separates perception from reasoning rather than learning them jointly.
AI.result: DiSR achieves competitive performance on popular spatial reasoning benchmarks without requiring large-scale 3D VQA training or complex tool-use policies. The framework also provides improved interpretability, modularity, and computational efficiency compared to end-to-end approaches.
AI.conclusion: Explicit separation of perception and reasoning is a scalable and effective alternative paradigm to end-to-end modeling for spatial intelligence. This disentangled approach leverages complementary strengths of specialized models while offering practical advantages in interpretability, modularity, and efficiency.

title: SkillTrace: Multi-Trace Provenance Auditing for LLM-Agent Skill Reuse
summary: LLM-agent ecosystems are rapidly growing around reusable skills: mixed-modality packages of metadata, natural-language instructions, code, tools, references, and operational workflows. As skills become marketplace artifacts, auditing their reuse is no longer the same problem as ordinary code clone detection. Existing detectors target single-modality source code or whole-package similarity, yet skill reuse evidence is distributed across authored text, implementation fragments, and operational structure. As a result, they can miss reuse that preserves only one part of a skill. We present SKILLTRACE, a multi-trace provenance auditing framework for LLM-agent skill reuse. SKILLTRACE extracts three provenance traces: Expression, Implementation, and Operational. It represents the Operational Trace as a Skill Operational Graph (SOG) that captures activation, procedure, and resource-flow structure. An LLM assists only the Operational-trace extraction, once at ingestion; at audit time SKILLTRACE compares cached traces deterministically, calibrates each trace against same-function strict negatives, and reports which trace supports a reuse decision. On SKILLTRACE-BENCH, with 820 transformed reuse positives over 100 marketplace anchors and 751 negative controls, SKILLTRACE achieves AUROC 0.938 and F1 0.898. A 36,446-skill wild audit further shows that trace-attributed evidence surfaces actionable reuse review queues beyond repository-level baselines.

AI.tldr: SKILLTRACE is a multi-trace provenance auditing framework that detects LLM-agent skill reuse by analyzing three provenance traces (Expression, Implementation, Operational), achieving high accuracy on benchmark testing and demonstrating practical value in real-world audits.
AI.motivation: Existing clone detection tools are inadequate for LLM-agent skill reuse auditing because they focus on single-modality source code or whole-package similarity, while skill reuse evidence is distributed across multiple modalities (text, code, operational structure). Current methods can miss reuse that preserves only partial skill components.
AI.method: SKILLTRACE extracts three provenance traces: Expression (metadata, instructions, references), Implementation (code fragments), and Operational (workflow structure). The Operational Trace is represented as a Skill Operational Graph (SOG) capturing activation, procedure, and resource-flow structure. LLM assistance is used only once during ingestion for Operational-trace extraction. At audit time, SKILLTRACE compares cached traces deterministically, calibrates each trace against strict negatives, and reports trace-specific evidence for reuse decisions.
AI.result: On SKILLTRACE-BENCH with 820 transformed reuse positives over 100 marketplace anchors and 751 negative controls, SKILLTRACE achieves AUROC 0.938 and F1 score 0.898. A wild audit of 36,446 skills shows that trace-attributed evidence surfaces actionable reuse review queues beyond repository-level baselines.
AI.conclusion: SKILLTRACE effectively addresses the multi-modal nature of LLM-agent skill reuse detection by using a multi-trace provenance approach. The framework provides trace-attributed evidence that enables more precise auditing than existing repository-level methods, making it valuable for marketplace skill quality control and reuse tracking.

title: Does Latent Context Help? A Controlled Evaluation of Inverse Reinforcement Learning in Arctic Shipping
summary: Artificial Intelligence (AI)-assisted navigation can help Arctic shipping adapt to rapidly changing sea-ice conditions, but reliable deployment requires reward models that are interpretable and robust to changing environments. Inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) provides a framework for recovering such rewards from vessel trajectories, while recent meta-IRL methods introduce latent context variables to capture behavioral heterogeneity. However, it remains unclear whether these latent representations recover genuinely hidden preferences or simply re-encode information already available in the observed state. We conduct a controlled evaluation on 3,186 AIS-derived voyages from 202 vessels across nine Arctic shipping seasons, comparing a linear shared reward, a nonlinear shared reward, and a latent-context model built on the same nonlinear architecture. The nonlinear reward improves held-out likelihood by 50.9% over the linear baseline, whereas adding vessel-specific latent context reduces performance by 16.5%. Behavioral analysis, context probes, and a pre-registered feature-hiding ablation show that apparent vessel-level variation is largely explained by observable route and environmental conditions rather than hidden vessel-specific factors. Moreover, predictive accuracy, route fidelity, and reward transfer yield different model rankings, demonstrating that no single metric is sufficient to evaluate learned rewards. These findings motivate testing whether the observed route, environmental, and vessel features already explain behavioral variation before adding per-vessel latent context. This supports more trustworthy AI deployment in safety-critical domains.

AI.tldr: While AI navigation helps Arctic shipping adapt to changing ice, reward models must be interpretable. Meta-IRL with latent context variables fails to capture hidden vessel preferences; observable route and environmental features already explain behavioral variation, questioning the need for per-vessel latent context.
AI.motivation: AI-assisted navigation can help Arctic shipping adapt to rapidly changing sea-ice conditions, but reliable deployment requires reward models that are interpretable and robust to changing environments. There's a need to understand whether latent context representations in meta-IRL methods recover genuinely hidden preferences or just re-encode observable information.
AI.method: Conducted controlled evaluation on 3,186 AIS-derived voyages from 202 vessels across nine Arctic shipping seasons. Compared three models: linear shared reward, nonlinear shared reward, and latent-context model built on same nonlinear architecture. Used behavioral analysis, context probes, and pre-registered feature-hiding ablation to understand what drives vessel-level variation.
AI.result: Nonlinear reward improved held-out likelihood by 50.9% over linear baseline, but adding vessel-specific latent context reduced performance by 16.5%. Behavioral variation was largely explained by observable route and environmental conditions rather than hidden vessel-specific factors. Predictive accuracy, route fidelity, and reward transfer gave different model rankings, showing no single metric suffices.
AI.conclusion: Observable route, environmental, and vessel features already explain behavioral variation, questioning the necessity of adding per-vessel latent context. These findings support testing whether observed features explain variation before adding latent context, promoting more trustworthy AI deployment in safety-critical domains like Arctic shipping.

title: Marginal Matching Does Not License Factorized Sampling: Auditing Conditional Style Leakage in Factorized Generative Models
summary:
Factorized generative models commonly regularize a latent style variable z_s by matching its marginal distribution to a fixed Gaussian prior and interpret this as evidence that the style representation is independent of class information. We show that this interpretation is incorrect. Matching only the marginal distribution places no constraint on the class-conditional distributions, allowing the latent style to remain highly predictive of the label despite appearing perfectly Gaussian in aggregate. We derive an exact decomposition showing that this mismatch is one of four conditions required for factorized sampling, and demonstrate that eliminating it is necessary but not sufficient to obtain the intended factorization.
  Empirically, our case-study model and four representative latent baselines achieve near-zero global MMD while still allowing a linear probe to recover class labels with 74%--100% accuracy (10% chance level). Our model reaches 99.15% clustering accuracy, whereas externally evaluated class-conditional generation succeeds only 16% of the time. This leakage remains under six independent perturbations involving model capacity, curriculum, prior geometry, and supervision across two datasets. Four mitigation strategies reduce probe accuracy to 21%--46%, although they leave within-class dependence largely unchanged. A post-hoc conditional prior improves externally evaluated class generation to 0.97 on MNIST without retraining but reaches only 0.41 on CIFAR-10, while an empirical style bank achieves 0.88 on CIFAR-10. These results demonstrate that no divergence computed solely on the marginal distribution of the style latent can certify independence from class labels, and that reporting marginal statistics alone does not verify the property commonly claimed in factorized generative models.

AI.tldr: Matching latent style distributions to Gaussian priors doesn't guarantee independence from class labels, as style can still be highly predictive of classes despite appearing Gaussian overall.
AI.motivation: Factorized generative models often claim style independence from class by matching marginal distributions to Gaussian priors, but this interpretation is flawed because marginal matching doesn't constrain class-conditional distributions.
AI.method: Derived an exact decomposition showing marginal mismatch is one of four conditions for factorized sampling. Empirically tested case-study model and four latent baselines with MMD metrics, linear probes, and perturbations across two datasets (MNIST and CIFAR-10). Evaluated mitigation strategies including conditional priors and empirical style banks.
AI.result: Models achieved near-zero global MMD but linear probes recovered class labels with 74%-100% accuracy (vs 10% chance). Style leakage persisted under six independent perturbations. Mitigation strategies reduced probe accuracy to 21%-46% but left within-class dependence largely unchanged. Conditional priors improved class generation to 0.97 on MNIST but only 0.41 on CIFAR-10.
AI.conclusion: No divergence computed solely on marginal distributions can certify independence from class labels. Reporting marginal statistics alone doesn't verify the property commonly claimed in factorized generative models, requiring examination of conditional distributions instead.

title: Abstract Event Causal Rules: Induction and Application
summary: Event-centric intelligent analytical systems heavily depend on explicit causal event knowledge for risk early warning, decision-making support and narrative comprehension. Nevertheless, existing instance-level causal pairs suffer severe generalization deficits on low-frequency long-tail and unseen event combinations. To address this limitation, this work proposes Abstract Event Causal Rule (AECR), a novel relation-level causal abstraction paradigm that transforms concrete cause-effect pairs into generalized abstract causal logic while retaining their intrinsic causal relationships. We design a multi-agent Concrete-to-Abstract Causal Induction (CACI) system coupled with similarity-constrained clustering to distill trustworthy AECRs from noisy raw causal data, based on which two complete AECR knowledge bases are built. To validate the practical utility of abstract causal knowledge, we propose an Abstract Rule-Guided Causal Attention Encoder (AR-GCAE), which injects the retrieved AECRs into the causality Graph Event Prediction (CGEP) benchmark task via rule-guided attention layers and gated representation fusion. Quantitative experimental results reveal that applying AECRs substantially strengthens the generalization capacity of event causal reasoning and brings consistent performance improvements to event prediction, with the most prominent gains observed on rare and unseen event samples.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Abstract Event Causal Rules (AECRs) - a novel relation-level causal abstraction paradigm that transforms specific event pairs into generalized causal logic to address generalization deficits in event causal reasoning.
AI.motivation: Existing instance-level causal event pairs suffer from severe generalization deficits, particularly for low-frequency long-tail and unseen event combinations, limiting the effectiveness of event-centric intelligent analytical systems that depend on explicit causal event knowledge.
AI.method: 1) Proposes Abstract Event Causal Rules (AECRs) as a relation-level causal abstraction paradigm; 2) Designs a multi-agent Concrete-to-Abstract Causal Induction (CACI) system with similarity-constrained clustering to distill trustworthy AECRs from noisy causal data; 3) Builds two complete AECR knowledge bases; 4) Proposes Abstract Rule-Guided Causal Attention Encoder (AR-GCAE) that injects retrieved AECRs into causality Graph Event Prediction tasks via rule-guided attention layers and gated representation fusion.
AI.result: Applying AECRs substantially strengthens the generalization capacity of event causal reasoning and brings consistent performance improvements to event prediction, with the most prominent gains observed on rare and unseen event samples in the causality Graph Event Prediction benchmark.
AI.conclusion: The abstract causal knowledge paradigm represented by AECRs effectively addresses generalization challenges in event causal reasoning, demonstrating practical utility for enhancing event prediction systems and analytical capabilities.

title: From Siloed Algorithms to Compliance-First Agentic Platforms: A Multi-Layered Architecture for Hospital AI Systems
summary: Hospitals are rapidly adopting artificial intelligence for triage, imaging, scheduling etc., yet most deployments remain isolated point solutions locked inside departmental silos, resulting in duplicated effort, hidden risks, and unrealized enterprise value. Despite explosive growth of AI in healthcare market and accelerating investment, an estimated 70-80% of healthcare AI pilots fail to scale, largely due to governance gaps, fragmented data, and missing integration blueprints. This research proposes a hospital-specific, compliance-first, Agentic AI architecture with multiple interoperable layers, extending existing hospital AI platform models with: (i) an Agent Orchestration Layer for multi-agent workflows across clinical, operational, and financial domains, (ii) a Compliance and Policy Layer that centralizes policy-as-code for HIPAA, GDPR, the EU AI Act, DISHA Act, India's DPDP Act, and ISO/IEC security and safety standards, and (iii) a Privacy-Preserving Data Fabric that plugs federated learning, differential privacy, and secure enclaves into real-world Hospital Information Management System (HIMS) flows. Using a synthetic but structurally realistic hospital dataset and an open, ready-to-deploy prototype implementation, this study demonstrates the end-to-end orchestration of triage risk prediction, workflow optimization, and compliance logging, achieving substantial simulated reductions in task turnaround times and manual documentation effort while maintaining policy-guarded data access. The resulting architecture offers hospital leaders a pragmatic blueprint to move from ad hoc tools to a governed, globally compliant, ROI-focused AI platform that can be tailored to on-premise, hybrid and cloud-native deployments.

AI.tldr: Proposes a comprehensive Agentic AI architecture for hospitals with integrated compliance layers and privacy-preserving data fabric to overcome fragmentation and scaling challenges in healthcare AI deployment.
AI.motivation: Current hospital AI deployments are isolated point solutions in departmental silos, leading to duplicated efforts, hidden risks, and unrealized enterprise value. 70-80% of healthcare AI pilots fail to scale due to governance gaps, fragmented data, and missing integration blueprints.
AI.method: Proposes a hospital-specific, compliance-first Agentic AI architecture with three key layers: 1) Agent Orchestration Layer for multi-agent workflows, 2) Compliance and Policy Layer centralizing policy-as-code for various regulations, and 3) Privacy-Preserving Data Fabric with federated learning, differential privacy, and secure enclaves integrated into HIMS flows. Tested using synthetic hospital dataset and open prototype implementation.
AI.result: Demonstrates end-to-end orchestration of triage risk prediction, workflow optimization, and compliance logging with substantial simulated reductions in task turnaround times and manual documentation effort while maintaining policy-guarded data access.
AI.conclusion: The architecture provides hospital leaders with a pragmatic blueprint to transition from ad hoc tools to a governed, globally compliant, ROI-focused AI platform adaptable to on-premise, hybrid, and cloud-native deployments.

title: PRISM: Priority-aware Rubric Internalization via Structured Multimodal Data Synthesis
summary: Real-world multimodal instructions often bundle multiple requirements with unequal importance, yet most multimodal training data still reduce instruction following to answering one self-contained question. We study this gap through \textbf{rubric comprehension}, which casts the model not as a generator measured against rubrics but as an \textbf{executor} that follows them: given an image and a typed, prioritized rubric, the model must verify each rule before producing an overall judgment. To support this setting, we propose \textbf{PRISM}, a four-stage data synthesis framework that produces persona--task pairs, prefix-guided rule sets, quality-filtered rubrics, and structured verification traces. We further introduce \textbf{PRISM-Eval}, whose Loose and Strict metrics use deterministic matching against fixed labels and therefore require no inference-time judge model. With only 10K synthesized samples, PRISM lifts Qwen3-VL-4B from 9.5\% to 30.1\% Strict accuracy on PRISM-Eval while preserving average performance on general benchmarks, and the gains transfer to four additional open-source MLLMs across dense and MoE architectures, suggesting that structured rubric supervision is a scalable path toward multi-rule, priority-aware multimodal instruction following.

AI.tldr: PRISM introduces a data synthesis framework for training multimodal models to follow prioritized rubrics with multiple requirements, improving rubric comprehension through structured verification rather than just answering questions.
AI.motivation: Real-world multimodal instructions often bundle multiple requirements with varying importance, but most training data only focuses on answering single self-contained questions, creating a gap between training and real-world application needs.
AI.method: Proposed PRISM - a four-stage data synthesis framework that: 1) generates persona-task pairs, 2) creates prefix-guided rule sets, 3) produces quality-filtered rubrics, and 4) generates structured verification traces. Also introduces PRISM-Eval with Loose and Strict metrics for evaluation.
AI.result: With only 10K synthesized samples, PRISM improved Qwen3-VL-4B from 9.5% to 30.1% Strict accuracy on PRISM-Eval while preserving average performance on general benchmarks. Gains transferred to four additional open-source MLLMs across different architectures.
AI.conclusion: Structured rubric supervision is a scalable path toward multi-rule, priority-aware multimodal instruction following, enabling models to act as executors that verify rubrics rather than just generators answering questions.

title: Otter: A Time-Aware, History-Conditioned Human Chess AI
summary:
Otter is a 15.3M-parameter human chess AI that predicts human move selection by modeling play as a time-aware, sequential process rather than treating each position in isolation. It combines two conditioning signals: (1) a move history encoder that conditions predictions on the last 20 moves, capturing opening preferences, positional drift, and intra-game behavioral tendencies; and (2) a time control module that modulates predictions based on clock pressure. Otter is trained on 6.1 billion positions from 117 million Lichess rapid games over 30 days on a single T4 GPU.
  Otter achieves 55.23% top-1 and 90.95% top-5 move-prediction accuracy, surpassing the prior state-of-the-art human chess model, Maia 2, with far fewer parameters and less training data. Across 11 Elo brackets (<1100 to >=2000), accuracy peaks at 57.38% in the 1900-1999 bracket. These results show that modeling chess as a time-aware, sequential activity yields more human-accurate move prediction than position-only approaches, using a smaller model. Code, trained models, and complete training logs are publicly released.

AI.tldr: Otter is a small (15.3M parameter) AI model that predicts human chess moves by considering move history and time control, outperforming larger models with less training data.
AI.motivation: Previous human chess AI models treated each chess position in isolation, ignoring important contextual factors like move history and time pressure that influence human decision-making in chess games.
AI.method: Otter uses a two-part conditioning approach: (1) a move history encoder that conditions predictions on the last 20 moves to capture opening preferences, positional drift, and intra-game behavior, and (2) a time control module that modulates predictions based on clock pressure. It was trained on 6.1 billion positions from 117 million Lichess rapid games.
AI.result: Achieved 55.23% top-1 and 90.95% top-5 move-prediction accuracy, surpassing the state-of-the-art Maia 2 model despite having far fewer parameters and less training data. Accuracy peaked at 57.38% in the 1900-1999 Elo bracket.
AI.conclusion: Modeling chess as a time-aware, sequential activity yields more human-accurate move prediction than position-only approaches, demonstrating that incorporating temporal and historical context is more important than simply scaling up model size.

title: Beyond Full-Model Rollback: AuroSFT for Adapter-State Multi-Task Fine-Tuning
summary: Multi-task supervised fine-tuning (SFT) often casts a heterogeneous data mixture as a single optimization problem, even though different tasks may reach their best generalization at different times. msft exposes this mismatch through task-wise roll-out, exclusion, and rollback, but its original formulation materializes the scheduler state as full-model checkpoints, making stage transitions costly to store, restore, and deploy. This paper introduces AuroSFT, a parameter-efficient framework that recasts the carried state of overfitting-aware multi-task SFT as a compact, mergeable adapter state. AuroSFT freezes the pretrained backbone, trains only injected adapters, rolls back adapter checkpoints at task-wise peaks, and continues on the remaining active mixture. At the layer level, each adapter applies an AuroRA-inspired adaptive nonlinear layer to a low-rank weight factor rather than to the sample representation. The resulting update remains linear in the input, rank-bounded, and exactly mergeable into the frozen projection. Under the retained-backbone comparison protocol, AuroSFT achieves 61.36% average accuracy, compared with 59.85% for the corresponding msft reference row, and obtains higher accuracy on all five backbones. Our code is available at the anonymous repository: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/AuroSFT-80D1.

AI.tldr: AuroSFT is a parameter-efficient framework that improves multi-task supervised fine-tuning by using compact, mergeable adapters instead of full-model checkpoints for task scheduling, achieving better accuracy with lower storage and deployment costs.
AI.motivation: Current multi-task SFT approaches treat heterogeneous data as a single optimization problem, but different tasks reach optimal generalization at different times. Existing solutions like msft use costly full-model checkpoints for task scheduling, making stage transitions expensive to store, restore, and deploy.
AI.method: AuroSFT freezes the pretrained backbone and trains only injected adapters. It uses task-wise roll-out, exclusion, and rollback with adapter checkpoints at task-wise peaks. Each adapter applies an AuroRA-inspired adaptive nonlinear layer to a low-rank weight factor, keeping updates linear in input, rank-bounded, and exactly mergeable into frozen projections.
AI.result: AuroSFT achieves 61.36% average accuracy compared to 59.85% for msft reference, and obtains higher accuracy on all five tested backbones under the retained-backbone comparison protocol.
AI.conclusion: AuroSFT provides an effective parameter-efficient solution for multi-task SFT by replacing costly full-model checkpoints with compact, mergeable adapter states, improving both accuracy and practical deployment efficiency.

title: SearchAuditor: Auditing and Attributing Failures in Long-Horizon Search Agents
summary: Deep search agents tackle challenging questions through long-horizon web interactions, a process that is both complex and fragile: small reasoning errors may propagate through long, noisy trajectories into fluent but incorrect answers. Diagnosing such failures is difficult, requiring the manual inspection of extremely long execution traces, which could be beyond human capacity. We therefore introduce SearchAuditBench, a benchmark that evaluates whether LLM auditors can localize, attribute, and repair these failures, thereby reducing the human burden. SearchAuditBench comprises 1,243 failed trajectories, averaging 73.1 messages and 65.1K tokens, collected from eight open-weight models on five deep-search benchmarks, each expert-annotated with the critical error step, a search-specific root cause, and a reference repair with grading rubrics. We further propose SearchAuditor, a multi-perspective auditing framework that effectively localizes, attributes, and repairs search-agent failures through evidence-grounded adjudication. Experimental results show that even the strongest baseline, when powered by a frontier model like GPT-5.5, attains only a 26.6% end-to-end pass rate. In contrast, our SearchAuditor consistently outperforms all baselines across different frontier models, achieving an end-to-end pass rate of 32.3%, and resuming failed runs with its repairs enables agents to better recover from errors.

AI.tldr: A benchmark (SearchAuditBench) and framework (SearchAuditor) for auditing and repairing failures in deep search agents through error localization, attribution, and repair.
AI.motivation: Deep search agents suffer from complex failures where small reasoning errors propagate through long, noisy trajectories, making diagnosis difficult due to extremely long execution traces that are hard for humans to inspect manually.
AI.method: Created SearchAuditBench with 1,243 failed trajectories (avg. 73.1 messages, 65.1K tokens) from eight models on five deep-search benchmarks, annotated with error steps, root causes, and repair references. Proposed SearchAuditor, a multi-perspective auditing framework using evidence-grounded adjudication for error localization, attribution, and repair.
AI.result: Strongest baseline (GPT-5.5) achieves only 26.6% end-to-end pass rate, while SearchAuditor achieves 32.3% end-to-end pass rate and enables agents to better recover from errors by resuming failed runs with repairs.
AI.conclusion: SearchAuditor provides an effective framework for auditing deep search agent failures, significantly outperforming baselines and reducing the human burden in diagnosing complex web interaction failures.

title: Beyond Rotations: AuroOFT for Expressive Quantized Orthogonal Fine-Tuning
summary: Quantized orthogonal fine-tuning (qoft) enables parameter-efficient adaptation of low-bit language models by learning structured activation rotations before frozen quantized weights. However, its task-specific updates remain constrained to linear orthogonal transformations, limiting input-dependent nonlinear corrections. We introduce AuroOFT, which keeps qoft as a stable quantization-compatible branch while attaching a zero-start gated low-rank nonlinear residual to each adapted linear layer. AuroOFT maps activations into an RMS-normalized compact latent space and uses adaptive nonlinear bases with bounded or token-dependent gating.
