The zero-initialized up projection makes AuroOFT functionally identical to qoft at initialization, while orthogonality remains a branch-level stability property rather than a property of the combined nonlinear layer. Under matched data, optimization, decoding, and parser protocols, AuroOFT improves Macro-6 over matched qoft by 1.30-2.70% on the 1.5B/3B Qwen2.5 settings, exceeds QLoRA by 6.52-10.62%, and saves 32.3-44.7% trainable parameters relative to QLoRA in representative scales. The small exam-style multiple-choice math set is treated only as a protocol-sensitivity diagnostic. Our code is available at the anonymous repository: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/AuroOFT-F3FD.

AI.tldr: AuroOFT enhances quantized orthogonal fine-tuning (qoft) by adding a zero-start gated low-rank nonlinear residual to each adapted linear layer, improving performance while maintaining quantization compatibility and parameter efficiency.
AI.motivation: While qoft enables parameter-efficient adaptation of low-bit language models, it's limited to linear orthogonal transformations, restricting input-dependent nonlinear corrections. The researchers aim to overcome this limitation while maintaining the quantization compatibility of qoft.
AI.method: AuroOFT keeps qoft as a stable branch and attaches a zero-start gated low-rank nonlinear residual to each adapted linear layer. It maps activations into RMS-normalized latent space and uses adaptive nonlinear bases with bounded or token-dependent gating. Zero-initialization ensures functional identity to qoft at initialization.
AI.result: Under matched protocols, AuroOFT improves Macro-6 over qoft by 1.30-2.70% on 1.5B/3B Qwen2.5 settings, exceeds QLoRA by 6.52-10.62%, and saves 32.3-44.7% trainable parameters relative to QLoRA. Small exam-style math sets served as protocol-sensitivity diagnostics.
AI.conclusion: AuroOFT successfully extends qoft's quantization-compatible adaptation framework to include nonlinear corrections, achieving superior performance while maintaining parameter efficiency and stability through its two-branch architecture.

title: PD-GS: Phoneme-Driven 3DGS for Audio-Driven Talking Heads
summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables fast, photorealistic talking-head rendering, yet accurate lip articulation remains elusive: mouth motion is often over-smoothed and may violate hard articulatory constraints such as bilabial closures, producing the notorious ``leaky mouth'' artifact. A key difficulty is that brief, discrete articulatory events are inferred from a continuous acoustic embedding under a regression objective, which biases predictions toward averaged mouth configurations. While modern self-supervised speech encoders provide rich prosodic and phonetic cues, they do not provide an explicit, frame-aligned linguistic target that reliably disambiguates closure-level events. We propose \textbf{Phoneme-Driven Gaussian Splatting (PD-GS)}, which augments a 3DGS talker with time-aligned phoneme tokens obtained from an automatic ASR and forced-alignment pipeline. Our core component, the \textbf{Linguistic Fusion Module (LFM)}, adaptively fuses continuous audio context with discrete phoneme embeddings through a learned gate, allowing the model to preserve smooth audio-driven dynamics while strengthening phoneme guidance on articulation-critical segments. PD-GS is trained purely from monocular video using image reconstruction and lip landmark supervision. On HDTF, PD-GS achieves the best lip geometry among the compared baselines (LMD 2.66) and qualitatively reduces closure violations in challenging phoneme sequences, yielding more linguistically faithful neural avatars.

AI.tldr: PD-GS improves 3DGS talking-head rendering by adding phoneme tokens and a Linguistic Fusion Module to address lip articulation issues like "leaky mouth" artifacts.
AI.motivation: Current 3D Gaussian Splatting for talking-head rendering produces inaccurate lip articulation with over-smoothed mouth motion and "leaky mouth" artifacts where bilabial closures are violated. The problem stems from continuous acoustic embeddings being insufficient for brief, discrete articulatory events like mouth closures.
AI.method: Proposes Phoneme-Driven Gaussian Splatting (PD-GS) which augments 3DGS with time-aligned phoneme tokens from ASR/forced-alignment pipeline. The core Linguistic Fusion Module (LFM) adaptively fuses continuous audio context with discrete phoneme embeddings through a learned gate to preserve smooth audio-driven dynamics while strengthening phoneme guidance on articulation-critical segments. Trained from monocular video using image reconstruction and lip landmark supervision.
AI.result: On HDTF dataset, PD-GS achieves best lip geometry among compared baselines (LMD 2.66) and qualitatively reduces closure violations in challenging phoneme sequences, producing more linguistically faithful neural avatars.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating explicit phoneme information via PD-GS successfully addresses the lip articulation limitations of 3DGS, particularly for brief articulatory events like closures, resulting in more accurate and natural talking-head rendering.

title: An Emerging Retail Portfolio Management Application: Personalized, Tax-Aware Reinforcement Learning with Natural Language Goals
summary: Retail investors lack access to the kind of personalized, tax-aware portfolio management that institutional clients take for granted -- existing robo-advisors use static, rule-based allocation, and institutional-grade systems require account minimums and technology stacks unavailable to individual investors. We present a fully built, integration-tested application that closes this gap: a FastAPI backend and web dashboard that let a user describe an investment goal in plain language (e.g. "I want steady growth but need to sell some shares next month for a down payment"), routes that goal to one of six investment mandates, and produces a live, broker-integrated portfolio recommendation from athree-phase reinforcement learning system -- a self-supervised cross-asset encoder, a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) allocation policy with a learned intent router, and a lightweight LoRA adapter that personalizes recommendations from an individual's revealed brokerage behavior without retraining the shared model. The system is functionally complete and integration-tested end-to-end against a live brokerage API (Alpaca, paper-trading mode), including multi-user authentication, a trust first preview-before-apply confirmation flow, daily email digests, and an auditable action-integrity chain, but has not yet been opened to real end-users; we report this honestly as an emerging, pre-deployment application with a concrete path to full deployment, alongside 14-day walk-forward backtests (bootstrapped confidence intervals included) as preliminary, pre-deployment validation rather than production performance. We also report several practical engineering lessons -- silently-inactive integration paths, hanging third-party API calls, and the value of end-to-end empirical verification over trusting checkpoint metadata -- that we believe generalize to other applied RL systems built on external, live data sources.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a production-ready robo-advisor system using reinforcement learning for personalized, tax-aware portfolio management accessible to retail investors, integrating with live brokerage APIs.
AI.motivation: Retail investors lack access to personalized, tax-aware portfolio management that institutions have; existing robo-advisors use static rule-based allocation, while institutional systems have high barriers to entry.
AI.method: Built a fully functional application with FastAPI backend and web dashboard that uses natural language goal input, routes to one of six investment mandates via a three-phase RL system: self-supervised cross-asset encoder, MoE allocation policy with learned intent router, and LoRA adapter for personalization from brokerage behavior. System includes multi-user auth, preview-confirmation flow, daily emails, and audit trail.
AI.result: System is functionally complete and integration-tested end-to-end against live brokerage API (Alpaca), with 14-day walk-forward backtests providing preliminary validation. Not yet deployed to real users but has concrete deployment path. Reported practical engineering lessons about silent failures, API issues, and value of empirical verification.
AI.conclusion: The system closes the gap in accessible personalized portfolio management for retail investors using RL, demonstrating practical integration with live brokerage systems while providing lessons for applied RL systems using external data sources.

title: When Privileged Guidance Misaligns: State-Matched Routing and Contextualized Self-Distillation for Multi-Turn Agents
summary: Privileged on-policy distillation provides dense supervision for multi-turn agents by allowing a synchronized teacher to re-score the student's response at every turn with access to training-only references, such as successful trajectories. In interactive environments, however, the student's preceding actions continually change the execution state. As the student takes different actions or completes subgoals in a different order, its rollout may reach states not covered by the reference, making the reference an unreliable source of guidance for the state actually reached. Applying privileged distillation indiscriminately therefore creates state--reference mismatch. This mismatch motivates a central objective: providing privileged reference guidance that remains compatible with the student's current execution state. We introduce State-Matched Routing and Contextualized Self-Distillation (SMRC-SD), which explicitly determines when and how a privileged trajectory should guide an on-policy student. At each turn, SMRC-SD verifies whether the student's current execution state matches a supported state along the reference trajectory. Distillation is applied only at matched states, filtering out turns for which the reference lacks locally compatible guidance. For each matched state, SMRC-SD further constructs state-conditioned teacher context from the successful trajectory, grounding supervision in the state actually reached. Across ALFWorld and WebShop, SMRC-SD consistently outperforms unconditional successful full-path distillation. With Qwen3-1.7B, it improves task success from $0.746$ to $0.865$ on ALFWorld and from $0.574$ to $0.693$ on WebShop. Controlled routing and context ablations support both selecting locally supported turns and constructing state-compatible teacher context as contributors to these gains. Code is available at https://github.com/liujunzhuo/SMRC-SD.

AI.tldr: SMRC-SD is a method that improves privileged distillation for multi-turn agents by only applying teacher guidance when the student's current state matches reference trajectory states, preventing state-reference mismatch.
AI.motivation: In interactive environments, privileged distillation can fail when the student's actions change the execution state differently than the reference trajectory, creating state-reference mismatch where the reference becomes unreliable for the actually reached state.
AI.method: State-Matched Routing and Contextualized Self-Distillation (SMRC-SD) verifies at each turn whether the student's current execution state matches a supported state along the reference trajectory, applying distillation only at matched states and constructing state-conditioned teacher context from successful trajectories.
AI.result: SMRC-SD improves task success from 0.746 to 0.865 on ALFWorld and from 0.574 to 0.693 on WebShop using Qwen3-1.7B, outperforming unconditional full-path distillation. Routing and context ablations show both components contribute to gains.
AI.conclusion: State-matching is crucial for effective privileged distillation in interactive environments. SMRC-SD provides a principled approach to ensure privileged guidance remains compatible with the student's actual execution state, significantly improving multi-turn agent performance.

title: Evaluating Machine Learning Models for Post-Wildfire Debris-Flow Prediction
summary: Prediction of post-wildfire debris flows is critical for mitigating hazards to communities, infrastructure, and resources during intense rainfall in recently burned areas. However, identifying reliable machine learning models is complicated by overlapping debris-flow and non-debris-flow events in feature space, the need for model interpretability, and limited training data. This paper addresses these challenges through a systematic evaluation of machine learning models in terms of predictive performance, feature importance, and synthetic data augmentation. Using basin-scale observations of post-wildfire debris-flow events across the western United States, we compare 15 models, including the Tabular Prior-Data Fitted Network (TabPFN). Repeated stratified cross-validation shows that TabPFN achieves the highest unaugmented performance with a threat score of 0.637, closely followed by the best tree-based models. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) are used to identify the features driving predictions, revealing that short-duration rainfall intensity and storm accumulation consistently rank highest, while burn severity and terrain features contribute less. We further evaluate synthetic data augmentation using TabPFN-generated samples to address the scarcity of debris-flow observations. Synthetic augmentation improves the performance of all models except CNN, with the largest mean threat score increase of +0.041 among the deep learning models. By combining rigorous model benchmarking, interpretable feature analysis, and synthetic data augmentation, this work provides a comprehensive framework for improving post-wildfire debris-flow prediction.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a systematic evaluation of machine learning models for predicting post-wildfire debris flows, finding TabPFN achieves best performance, with SHAP analysis showing rainfall intensity as most important, and synthetic data augmentation improves most models.
AI.motivation: Predicting post-wildfire debris flows is critical for hazard mitigation during intense rainfall in burned areas, but current approaches face challenges including overlapping event classes in feature space, need for model interpretability, and limited training data.
AI.method: Systematically evaluated 15 ML models including TabPFN using basin-scale observations across western US, with repeated stratified cross-validation. Used SHAP for feature importance analysis and implemented synthetic data augmentation using TabPFN-generated samples to address data scarcity.
AI.result: TabPFN achieved highest unaugmented performance with threat score of 0.637. SHAP analysis showed short-duration rainfall intensity and storm accumulation consistently rank highest in importance, while burn severity and terrain features contribute less. Synthetic augmentation improved all models except CNN, with deep learning models showing largest mean threat score increase of +0.041.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a comprehensive framework combining rigorous model benchmarking, interpretable feature analysis, and synthetic data augmentation to improve post-wildfire debris-flow prediction, addressing key challenges in this critical hazard mitigation task.

title: Small Foundation Models of Human Cognition and Behaviour
comment: published as a conference paper at COLM'26
summary: Large language models fine-tuned on human behavioural data have emerged as general-purpose cognitive proxies, but the scale this requires, and whether these models process task structure or exploit statistical shortcuts, remain open questions. We train fourteen models from 135M to 14B parameters across four architecture families on Psych-101, a dataset of 10.7 million trial-level choices from 160 experiments. In-distribution, scale barely matters. The models fall within a narrow band, as though against a ceiling, and 0.6B to 1B parameters suffice to match a 70B baseline on held-out participants. Out-of-distribution, that band opens into a markedly steeper scaling gradient, with larger models clearly advantaged in generalisation to novel task structure. To determine what information these models use, we run two diagnostics. We progressively strip four prompt channels -- task instructions, experimental stimuli, outcome feedback, and choice history -- across 27 experiments, and permute trial order. Masking the content of stimuli and feedback destroys 75.7% of learned information and pushes models below chance, demonstrating that choice history alone does not account for performance. Permutation reveals invariance on tasks with independent trials but sensitivity where trial order is determined by prior responses. Small cognitively fine-tuned models therefore show promise as noise ceiling estimators for psychological experiments, though their scope remains bounded by the paradigms seen in training.

AI.tldr: Fine-tuned LLMs trained on behavioral data reach performance ceilings around 0.6B-1B parameters for in-distribution tasks, but scale matters for generalization to novel task structures, with larger models benefiting from content beyond just choice history patterns.
AI.motivation: To understand whether fine-tuned LLMs processing human behavioral data learn actual task structure or just exploit statistical shortcuts, and to determine the scale requirements and information sources for such cognitive proxies.
AI.method: Trained 14 models (135M to 14B parameters across 4 architectures) on Psych-101 dataset with 10.7M trial-level choices from 160 experiments; conducted ablation studies by progressively stripping prompt channels (instructions, stimuli, feedback, choice history) and permuting trial order to determine information sources.
AI.result: In-distribution performance shows minimal scaling effects (0.6B-1B parameters match 70B baseline), suggesting a performance ceiling. Out-of-distribution, larger models clearly excel at generalization. Stripping stimuli and feedback destroys 75.7% of learned information, showing models use more than just choice history patterns.
AI.conclusion: Small fine-tuned LLMs (~0.6B-1B parameters) can serve as effective noise ceiling estimators for psychological experiments, but their generalization remains bounded by training paradigms, and they learn from meaningful content beyond mere choice history patterns.

title: Rectifying Geometric Misalignment: Online Source-Free Adaptation for Class-Imbalanced EEG
summary: Electroencephalography (EEG) based Brain-Computer Interfaces (BCIs) often require unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) to generalize across subjects and sessions. While Riemannian alignment methods like the Riemannian Centering Transformation (RCT) are effective for handling covariate shifts, they implicitly assume balanced class priors. However, in realistic online BCI scenarios, the label distributions vary dynamically (label shift), causing standard alignment techniques to geometrically misalign the target data distributions. In this work, we propose OSPDIM (Online SPD manifold information maximization), a source-free online UDA framework designed to address label shifts on the Riemannian manifold. OSPDIM introduces a manifold-constrained bias parameter into the tangent space mapping, which is optimized via information maximization to correct the geometric skew caused by imbalanced data streams. Unlike offline methods relying on global batch statistics, OSPDIM estimates and corrects geometric bias on-the-fly. Simulations on 2D SPD matrices visually demonstrate that OSPDIM successfully rectifies the misalignment where standard centering fails. Extensive experiments on multiple motor imagery datasets show that OSPDIM significantly outperforms standard Riemannian baselines, particularly in challenging online adaptation scenarios with severe class imbalance, offering a robust solution for practical, plug-and-play BCI systems.

AI.tldr: OSPDIM is a novel online unsupervised domain adaptation framework that addresses label shifts in EEG-based BCIs by correcting geometric misalignment on Riemannian manifolds through information maximization and manifold-constrained bias parameters.
AI.motivation: Traditional Riemannian alignment methods for EEG-based BCIs assume balanced class priors, but real-world online BCI scenarios experience dynamic label shifts (class imbalance) that cause geometric misalignment of target data distributions when using standard alignment techniques like Riemannian Centering Transformation.
AI.method: OSPDIM introduces a source-free online UDA framework with a manifold-constrained bias parameter in tangent space mapping. It optimizes this bias via information maximization to correct geometric skew from imbalanced data streams. Unlike offline methods using global batch statistics, OSPDIM estimates and corrects geometric bias on-the-fly during online operation.
AI.result: Simulations on 2D SPD matrices show OSPDIM successfully rectifies misalignment where standard centering fails. Extensive experiments on multiple motor imagery datasets demonstrate OSPDIM significantly outperforms standard Riemannian baselines, especially in challenging online adaptation scenarios with severe class imbalance.
AI.conclusion: OSPDIM provides a robust, plug-and-play solution for practical BCI systems by effectively addressing label shifts in online adaptation scenarios through geometric bias correction on Riemannian manifolds.

title: Project2Task: Graph-Guided Project-Level Planning for Autonomous Research
summary: Research agents can increasingly search literature, propose hypotheses, generate code, run experiments, and draft manuscripts from a single topic. However, a research project is not merely a larger task: it is a long-horizon agenda that must be advanced through multiple bounded tasks with distinct but related objectives, parallel alternatives, and dependency-aware sequences. Existing single-task systems often treat the project as one oversized task, produce a flat set of vague or overlapping tasks, or leave task boundaries and execution order to manual coordination. We introduce Project2Task, a graph-guided project-level planning layer for autonomous research. Given a project brief, it represents candidate contributions as innovation atoms and organizes them in a directed lineage graph. A lightweight Bernoulli block-model objective selects among horizontal, vertical, and hybrid portfolio decompositions. Project2Task then generates bounded tasks with explicit contribution ownership, repairs overlaps and missing execution fields, and emits dependency-aware task contracts that specify objectives, inputs, expected artifacts, evaluation requirements, boundary constraints, dependencies, and execution order. The contracts are independent of any particular downstream research executor and support integration of task outputs into a coherent project-level result. On a benchmark of ten project briefs yielding roughly 30 tasks, manuscript-based portfolio evaluation gives Project2Task an average quality score of 7.15, compared with 4.58 for the Brief Baseline and 5.31 for the Topic-only Setting. Integrating its contracts with AutoResearchClaw increases average downstream task accuracy from 0.536 to 0.759. These results demonstrate the value of explicit project-to-task planning for producing coherent, non-redundant, and executable research-task portfolios.

AI.tldr: Project2Task introduces a graph-guided planning system that decomposes research projects into coherent, non-redundant, executable task portfolios with explicit dependencies, improving research quality and downstream task execution.
AI.motivation: Current research agents often treat entire projects as single oversized tasks, produce flat/vague task sets, or require manual coordination, failing to capture the complex structure of research projects involving multiple bounded tasks with distinct objectives, parallel alternatives, and dependency-aware sequences.
AI.method: Project2Task represents candidate contributions as innovation atoms organized in a directed lineage graph, uses a Bernoulli block-model objective to select horizontal/vertical/hybrid portfolio decompositions, generates bounded tasks with explicit ownership, repairs overlaps, and produces dependency-aware task contracts specifying objectives, inputs, artifacts, evaluation, constraints, dependencies, and execution order.
AI.result: On 10 project briefs (≈30 tasks), Project2Task achieved average quality score of 7.15 vs 4.58 for Brief Baseline and 5.31 for Topic-only Setting. Integrating with AutoResearchClaw increased downstream task accuracy from 0.536 to 0.759.
AI.conclusion: The results demonstrate that explicit project-to-task planning significantly improves research quality by producing coherent, non-redundant, and executable task portfolios, highlighting the importance of structured decomposition for autonomous research systems.

title: QEvict: Recoverable Quantized KV Eviction for Attention-Drift-Robust Long-Context Decoding
comment: 24 pages, 6 figures. The first four authors contributed equally
summary: Autoregressive large language model inference is increasingly constrained by the memory footprint of the Key-Value (KV) cache. A dominant line of work reduces this footprint by evicting tokens that appear unimportant under attention-derived scores. However, such policies make an implicit irreversible decision: once a token is evicted, it cannot become useful again. We show that this assumption is brittle during decoding. Token and window importance drift as generated queries evolve, causing standard eviction policies to permanently discard states that later receive substantial attention under the full-cache model. To characterize this behaviour, we introduce Future Missed Mass and Global LIR, two diagnostics that measure future attention assigned to discarded states and the reactivation of historically inactive regions. We propose QEvict, a three-tier KV-cache management scheme that replaces binary retain-or-delete eviction with recoverable eviction. QEvict maintains high-confidence windows in full precision, stores intermediate windows in a quantized recoverable tier, and deletes only the lowest-confidence windows. During decoding, cumulative attention scores update window importance and when a quantized window becomes important again, it is dequantized and promoted to the full-precision. Under a fixed memory budget, this design preserves broader historical context while retaining exact full precision for the most important regions. Across long-context understanding, retrieval, and reasoning benchmarks, QEvict consistently improves over representative eviction and quantization baselines, reducing missed attention and improving information retention

AI.tldr: QEvict: A three-tier KV-cache management scheme that uses recoverable eviction instead of binary retain/delete decisions, storing intermediate windows in quantized form for potential reactivation, improving memory efficiency while preserving important context.
AI.motivation: Current KV-cache eviction methods permanently discard tokens deemed unimportant, but this is problematic because token importance can change during decoding as generated queries evolve - previously unimportant tokens can become important later under the full-cache model.
AI.method: Proposes QEvict with three tiers: 1) high-confidence windows kept in full precision, 2) intermediate windows stored in quantized recoverable tier, 3) lowest-confidence windows deleted. Uses cumulative attention scores to track window importance, with quantized windows being dequantized and promoted when they become important again.
AI.result: QEvict reduces missed attention and improves information retention across long-context understanding, retrieval, and reasoning benchmarks, consistently outperforming representative eviction and quantization baselines under fixed memory budgets.
AI.conclusion: The irreversible binary eviction assumption is brittle; recoverable eviction via quantization preserves broader historical context while maintaining exact full precision for important regions, making KV-cache management more adaptive to changing token importance during decoding.

title: TriQua: Reconciling Granularity and Context in Factuality Evaluation
summary: The "decompose-then-verify" paradigm for LLM factuality evaluation faces a fundamental trade-off: atomic facts, i.e., one sentence conveying one unit of information, often omit essential context, while broader statements lack the granularity needed for precise assessment. To address this, we introduce TriQua, a framework that flexibly models facts based on their complexity. Simple claims are extracted as standard triples, while complex claims are represented as hyperrelational facts by attaching auxiliary contextual qualifiers. This adaptive structure preserves the necessary context for accurate retrieval and verification without sacrificing atomicity. Furthermore, TriQua's verification process directly annotates concrete errors within specific triples and qualifiers, providing fine-grained explainability for error detection. Alongside the framework, we propose TriQuaScore to quantify the factuality of these structured fact units. Empirical evaluations show that TriQuaScore strongly aligns with human annotated factuality scores, TriQua achieves robust decomposition quality, and outperforms existing decomposition-based frameworks in evidence-based fact verification.

AI.tldr: TriQua is a flexible framework for LLM factuality evaluation that adapts between atomic facts (simple triples) and complex facts (hyperrelational facts with qualifiers) to balance context preservation and granularity, with improved verification and explainability.
AI.motivation: The "decompose-then-verify" paradigm for LLM factuality evaluation faces a fundamental trade-off: atomic facts (single-sentence units) often omit essential context, while broader statements lack the granularity needed for precise assessment.
AI.method: Introduces TriQua framework that flexibly models facts based on complexity: simple claims as standard triples (subject-predicate-object), complex claims as hyperrelational facts with auxiliary contextual qualifiers. Uses adaptive structure to preserve necessary context without sacrificing atomicity. Verification process directly annotates concrete errors within specific triples and qualifiers. Also proposes TriQuaScore to quantify factuality of structured fact units.
AI.result: Empirical evaluations show: 1) TriQuaScore strongly aligns with human annotated factuality scores, 2) TriQua achieves robust decomposition quality, 3) TriQua outperforms existing decomposition-based frameworks in evidence-based fact verification.
AI.conclusion: TriQua successfully addresses the granularity-context trade-off in LLM factuality evaluation through adaptive fact modeling, providing fine-grained explainability and improved verification performance compared to existing approaches.

title: DG-FedReuse: Proxy-Gradient-Gated Cached-Update Reuse with Matched Sparse Uplink Accounting
summary: Federated learning repeatedly incurs local optimization and model-update transmission. We study DG-FedReuse, a simulator-level mechanism that allows selected clients to contribute age-decayed cached updates when a stochastic head-gradient discrepancy proxy remains below a round-dependent threshold. A hard cache-age limit and minimum fresh-client quota constrain reuse, while fresh updates use an adaptive per-tensor Top-K numerical-field representation. Experiments cover six image-classification datasets, 50 virtual clients, Dirichlet label heterogeneity (α=0.5), and three seeds. At a common 90-round budget, DG-FedReuse yields 83.36-85.42% modeled update-data-field uplink saving, compared with 76.88% for matched Top-K FedAvg; the seed-aligned accuracy differences range from -5.29 to -0.14 percentage points. Best-observed test accuracies obtained under test-controlled checkpointing are retained only as exploratory archival evidence and range from -2.38 to +0.45 percentage points relative to matched FedAvg. A symmetric dense-model-downlink sensitivity reduces the headline saving to 41.68-F42.71% and the incremental gain over Top-K FedAvg to 3.24-4.27 percentage points, demonstrating the dependence of communication conclusions on the accounting boundary. The study characterizes the proposed reuse rule in the implemented simulator; it does not establish unbiased generalization, end-to-end bandwidth reduction, runtime or energy savings, faster convergence, or superiority over existing stale-update and lazy-aggregation methods.

AI.tldr: DG-FedReuse reduces federated learning communication costs by reusing cached client updates when they're still useful, achieving significant uplink savings with minimal accuracy loss.
AI.motivation: Federated learning requires frequent local optimization and model-update transmission, which creates significant communication overhead. The paper aims to reduce this overhead by intelligently reusing cached client updates when they remain sufficiently relevant, rather than requiring fresh updates every round.
AI.method: The proposed DG-FedReuse mechanism allows selected clients to contribute age-decayed cached updates instead of fresh ones when a stochastic head-gradient discrepancy proxy stays below a round-dependent threshold. It includes: 1) a hard cache-age limit, 2) minimum fresh-client quota constraint, and 3) adaptive per-tensor Top-K numerical-field representation for fresh updates. The method was evaluated on six image-classification datasets with 50 virtual clients and Dirichlet label heterogeneity.
AI.result: At 90-round budget: 83.36-85.42% uplink savings in modeled update-data fields compared to 76.88% for matched Top-K FedAvg. Accuracy differences range from -5.29 to -0.14 percentage points. Best-observed test accuracies range from -2.38 to +0.45 percentage points relative to matched FedAvg. When accounting for symmetric dense-model-downlink, savings reduce to 41.68-42.71% with incremental gain of 3.24-4.27 percentage points over Top-K FedAvg.
AI.conclusion: DG-FedReuse effectively reduces communication costs in federated learning by reusing cached updates while maintaining reasonable accuracy, though communication savings conclusions depend heavily on accounting boundaries. The study only characterizes the proposed reuse rule in a simulator and doesn't establish unbiased generalization, end-to-end bandwidth reduction, runtime/energy savings, faster convergence, or superiority over existing stale-update methods.

title: Coherence-Oriented Dream Scene Visualisation
summary: Dreams can be emotionally intense but difficult to communicate. We describe the Dream Scene Visualiser (DSV) system which turns written dream descriptions into a temporal sequence of four panel images visualising the dream. This starts with a large language model prompted to split a dream description into four chronological parts. Then a text-to-image model produces images for each part with visual coherence maintained across the sequence, and DSV regenerates any image not suitably matching the text. We evaluate DSV over 50 visualisations from dream descriptions in DreamBank, and report quality, fidelity and coherence results via objective measures employing the CLIP, DINOv2 and Qwen2-VL vision-language models.

AI.tldr: Dream Scene Visualiser (DSV) converts written dream descriptions into 4-panel visual sequences using LLMs for temporal splitting and text-to-image models for generation, with evaluation on dream databases using vision-language models.
AI.motivation: Dreams are emotionally intense experiences but difficult to communicate and share with others effectively through text alone.
AI.method: DSV uses a large language model to split dream descriptions into four chronological parts, then text-to-image models generate images for each part with visual coherence maintenance, regenerating images that don't match text.
AI.result: Evaluated over 50 visualizations from DreamBank dream descriptions, reporting quality, fidelity, and coherence results using objective measures from CLIP, DINOv2, and Qwen2-VL vision-language models.
AI.conclusion: The DSV system provides an automated way to visualize dream narratives as temporal image sequences, potentially making dream communication more accessible and engaging.

title: Quantum-Structured World Models (QSWMs) for Predictive Latent Dynamics
summary: World models learn latent states that summarize interaction histories, evolve over time, and support prediction, simulation, or planning. Most existing world models represent these states using classical vectors, probability distributions, recurrent hidden states, or transformer activations. In this paper, we introduce Quantum-Structured World Models (QSWMs), a quantum-inspired framework for predictive world modeling with structured latent states, latent transition operators, and measurement-inspired decoding maps. We study whether mathematical structures inspired by quantum theory, such as complex-valued representations and density-matrix-like latents, provide useful inductive biases for world modeling. We establish three foundational properties: classical inclusion, predictive sufficiency, and structured compactness. We then instantiate complex-valued and density-matrix-like QSWM variants and evaluate them on elementary cellular automata against strong classical baselines. Results show promising local predictive potential for complex-valued QSWMs, while also revealing limitations in long-horizon rollout, density-matrix variants

AI.tldr: Quantum-Structured World Models (QSWMs) introduce a quantum-inspired framework for world modeling using complex-valued representations and density-matrix-like latent states, showing promising local predictive potential but limitations in long-horizon rollouts.
AI.motivation: Most existing world models use classical representations (vectors, distributions, recurrent states, or transformer activations), but the paper explores whether mathematical structures inspired by quantum theory can provide better inductive biases for world modeling.
AI.method: Introduce QSWMs with structured latent states, latent transition operators, and measurement-inspired decoding maps based on quantum theory concepts. Study complex-valued representations and density-matrix-like latents. Establish three foundational properties: classical inclusion, predictive sufficiency, and structured compactness. Instantiate and evaluate complex-valued and density-matrix QSWM variants.
AI.result: QSWMs show promising local predictive potential for complex-valued variants on elementary cellular automata tasks, but reveal limitations in long-horizon rollout performance, particularly for density-matrix variants.
AI.conclusion: Quantum-inspired structures like complex-valued representations and density-matrix-like latents offer useful inductive biases for world modeling, though current implementations have limitations in long-horizon prediction that require further research.

title: Search2Skill: Skill Distillation Beyond Knowledge Boundaries Via Rubric-Based Reinforcement Learning
summary: Reusable skills, which encapsulate the procedural knowledge required to solve real-world professional tasks, offer LLM-based agents a path toward self-evolution in expert domains. Existing self-evolving skill methods construct skills internally from the model's parametric knowledge or trajectories, and are therefore bounded by what the model already knows. However, the domain conventions and standard procedures underlying professional skills often lie beyond this boundary and are hard to elicit from the agent alone. To address this issue, we therefore propose a novel framework, Search2Skill, that automatically identifies the agent's capability gaps, searches external sources to address them, and distills the retrieved evidence into structured, reusable skills. Specifically, Search2Skill is optimized by a rubric-based reinforcement learning scheme that jointly improves when to search, how to search, and how to generate skills. Experiments on eight expert-level domains from three benchmarks show that Search2Skill consistently outperforms both search-augmented and trajectory-based skill-learning baselines under both streaming and held-out evaluation protocols. Further analyses show that the gains arise from skill abstraction rather than raw retrieved evidence, and that the acquired skills transfer across model scales.

AI.tldr: Search2Skill enables LLM agents to autonomously evolve expert skills by identifying knowledge gaps, searching external sources, and distilling findings into reusable structured skills via rubric-based reinforcement learning, outperforming existing methods across multiple domains.
AI.motivation: Current self-evolving skill methods for LLM-based agents are limited because they only construct skills from the model's existing parametric knowledge or trajectories, which cannot capture professional domain conventions and standard procedures that lie beyond what the model already knows. These external professional skills are hard to elicit from the agent alone, creating a fundamental limitation in agent self-evolution.
AI.method: Search2Skill is a novel framework that automatically identifies the agent's capability gaps, searches external sources (like documents, databases, or the web) to address these gaps, and distills the retrieved evidence into structured, reusable skills. The framework is optimized by a rubric-based reinforcement learning scheme that jointly improves three key components: when to search (timing), how to search (search strategy), and how to generate skills from the retrieved information.
AI.result: Experiments across eight expert-level domains from three benchmarks show that Search2Skill consistently outperforms both search-augmented baselines (that just use raw retrieved information) and trajectory-based skill-learning baselines. This performance advantage holds under both streaming (incremental) and held-out (separate test) evaluation protocols. Additional analyses reveal that the gains come from skill abstraction rather than just using raw retrieved evidence, and that the acquired skills successfully transfer across different model scales.
AI.conclusion: Search2Skill represents a significant advancement in enabling LLM agents to evolve professional expertise by going beyond their internal knowledge boundaries through systematic external knowledge acquisition and skill distillation. The framework's ability to create structured, reusable skills from external sources addresses a fundamental limitation in agent self-evolution and demonstrates practical effectiveness across diverse expert domains.

title: Spectral Distillation: From Nonlinear Dynamics to Linear State-Space Models
summary: Can nonlinear dynamical systems be learned through a compact linear state-space representation, without directly solving a non-convex system-identification problem? We give a provable pipeline for doing so. Starting from observations of an unknown nonlinear dynamical system, we first learn an implicit spectral predictor using Observation Spectral Filtering (OSF), a convex method that competes with the best linear observer for the system. We then apply spectral-to-LDS distillation to convert this predictor into an explicit recurrent linear dynamical system. Our main theorem shows that the average prediction error of the distilled LDS decomposes into an exponentially-small distillation term and the OSF learning term governed by the Luenberger complexity of the best observer. The guarantee is dimension-free: it depends on observer complexity rather than on the latent dimension needed to represent the nonlinear system. To our knowledge, this yields the first end-to-end provable method for extracting a best-in-hindsight LDS representation of nonlinear dynamics through convex learning followed by provable distillation. Experiments on linear LDS benchmarks and MuJoCo behavior cloning show that the train-then-distill pipeline produces compact LDS predictors that match or outperform directly trained baselines.

AI.tldr: A provable method for learning compact linear state-space representations of nonlinear dynamical systems using convex learning (OSF) followed by distillation, achieving dimension-free guarantees based on observer complexity rather than system dimension.
AI.motivation: Learning nonlinear dynamical systems directly often involves solving non-convex system identification problems, which is challenging. The paper aims to provide a provable method for extracting linear state-space representations from nonlinear dynamics without solving these difficult non-convex problems.
AI.method: Two-stage approach: 1) Learn an implicit spectral predictor using Observation Spectral Filtering (OSF), a convex method that competes with the best linear observer. 2) Apply spectral-to-LDS distillation to convert this predictor into an explicit recurrent linear dynamical system.
AI.result: The main theorem shows average prediction error decomposes into exponentially-small distillation term plus OSF learning term governed by Luenberger complexity of the best observer. The guarantee is dimension-free (depends on observer complexity, not latent dimension). Experiments on linear LDS benchmarks and MuJoCo behavior cloning show the pipeline produces compact LDS predictors matching or outperforming directly trained baselines.
AI.conclusion: The paper presents the first end-to-end provable method for extracting best-in-hindsight LDS representations of nonlinear dynamics through convex learning followed by provable distillation, offering dimension-free guarantees and practical effectiveness.

title: LUNAR: Benchmarking Personalized Large Language Models on UNiversal User BehAvioR Logs
summary: Existing personalized LLM benchmarks primarily rely on textual personas or isolated behavioral signals, providing limited evaluation of cross-domain behavioral personalization, where responses must be grounded in heterogeneous daily-life activities. To address this gap, we introduce LUNAR, the first benchmark for evaluating how LLMs personalize responses from longitudinal app interaction histories across universal daily-life domains, including clothing, food, housing, and mobility. To support scalable benchmark construction while mitigating data sparsity and privacy concerns, LUNAR uses a multi-stage coarse-to-fine synthesis pipeline grounded in real-world behavioral patterns. Fidelity analyses show closer alignment with real behavioral distributions than other synthetic benchmarks. Experiments on 19 mainstream LLMs show that access to behavioral logs is necessary but not sufficient for deep personalization: neither more context nor larger models guarantees better performance; effective personalization depends on selecting and integrating relevant evidence across domains. Direct retrieval of fine-grained behavioral records consistently outperforms compressed memory, while stronger personalization can come at the cost of privacy protection. These findings identify evidence selection, cross-domain integration, and privacy control as key challenges for personalized LLMs.

AI.tldr: LUNAR is the first benchmark for evaluating LLM personalization based on longitudinal app interaction histories across daily-life domains (clothing, food, housing, mobility), showing that behavioral logs are necessary but not sufficient for deep personalization.
AI.motivation: Existing personalized LLM benchmarks rely on textual personas or isolated behavioral signals, providing limited evaluation of cross-domain behavioral personalization grounded in heterogeneous daily-life activities.
AI.method: LUNAR uses a multi-stage coarse-to-fine synthesis pipeline grounded in real-world behavioral patterns to construct benchmarks while mitigating data sparsity and privacy concerns. Experiments on 19 mainstream LLMs evaluate their ability to personalize responses from app interaction histories.
AI.result: Access to behavioral logs is necessary but not sufficient for deep personalization. More context or larger models don't guarantee better performance. Direct retrieval of fine-grained behavioral records outperforms compressed memory, but stronger personalization can compromise privacy protection.
AI.conclusion: Evidence selection, cross-domain integration, and privacy control are key challenges for personalized LLMs, as effective personalization depends on selecting and integrating relevant evidence across domains while balancing privacy concerns.

title: Perturbation Sensitivity at Convergence: A Simple Signal for Identifying Spuriously Correlated Samples
summary: Models trained by empirical risk minimization on data containing spurious correlations achieve high average accuracy while failing on subpopulations where the correlation does not hold. Existing methods for identifying the affected samples without group annotations rely on signals from early training, which requires locating the epoch at which to intervene, a hyperparameter typically selected using group-labeled validation data. We show that a usable signal is available after convergence, when loss no longer distinguishes the two populations. Samples consistent with the spurious correlation are classified by a shared rule, while the remaining samples are fit through configurations specific to individual inputs and are correspondingly more fragile. Applying a fixed perturbation to a converged model's inputs flips the predictions of the latter far more often than the former. The resulting procedure requires two forward passes per training sample, no group annotations at any stage, and no early-stopping epoch. Using the detected samples to rebalance training raises worst-group accuracy on Waterbirds from 57.3% to 80.8%, against 85.8% with ground-truth group labels.

AI.tldr: A method to identify spurious correlation samples without group labels by analyzing model fragility to input perturbations after convergence, improving worst-group accuracy without needing early training intervention or group annotations.
AI.motivation: Models trained with empirical risk minimization often fail on minority subpopulations where spurious correlations don't hold. Existing methods need group-labeled validation data and require identifying the optimal training epoch for intervention, which is problematic when group annotations are unavailable.
AI.method: After model convergence when loss no longer distinguishes populations, apply fixed perturbations to inputs and observe prediction changes. Samples fitting spurious correlations (majority) are robust while minority samples are fragile. Use this fragility signal to identify affected samples without group labels or early-stopping epoch selection.
AI.result: On Waterbirds dataset, the method raises worst-group accuracy from 57.3% to 80.8% using detected samples for rebalanced training, compared to 85.8% with ground-truth group labels. Requires only two forward passes per sample and no group annotations at any stage.
AI.conclusion: Model fragility to perturbations after convergence provides a reliable signal to identify samples affected by spurious correlations, enabling effective debiasing without group annotations or complex hyperparameter tuning, significantly improving worst-group performance.

title: WorldClaw: Agentic 3D Open-World Generation at Scale
comment: Authors are listed in alphabetical order by given name
summary: Generating large-scale, freely explorable 3D worlds from open-ended text remains challenging because a system must jointly maintain global spatial coherence, rich local content, and explicit assets suitable for downstream editing and reuse. We present WorldClaw, a fully agentic, coarse-to-fine framework for open-world 3D scene generation. Planning agents translate a text prompt into a structured specification of regions, terrain, assets, materials, and spatial relations. WorldClaw then builds a globally coherent terrain foundation from semantic layouts, reusable assets, generative or procedural materials, and a region-aware height field. For detail-demanding regions, it generates terrain-conditioned compositions, reconstructs editable textured meshes, and recovers their placement on the terrain; render-based agents further refine terrain, objects, appearance, and contacts. Across diverse open-world prompts, WorldClaw produces large-scale scenes with coherent spatial organization, visually compelling local content, and editable instance-level assets while preserving a consistent global terrain structure.

AI.tldr: WorldClaw is an agentic framework that generates large-scale 3D worlds from text by using planning agents to create structured specifications and building coherent terrains with editable assets.
AI.motivation: Current methods struggle to generate large-scale 3D worlds that maintain global spatial coherence, rich local content, and explicit editable assets suitable for downstream editing from open-ended text prompts.
AI.method: WorldClaw uses planning agents to translate text prompts into structured specifications of regions, terrain, assets, materials, and spatial relations. It builds globally coherent terrain foundations from semantic layouts, reusable assets, generative/procedural materials, and region-aware height fields. For detail-demanding regions, it generates terrain-conditioned compositions, reconstructs editable textured meshes, and recovers their placement on terrain. Render-based agents further refine terrain, objects, appearance, and contacts.
AI.result: Across diverse open-world prompts, WorldClaw produces large-scale scenes with coherent spatial organization, visually compelling local content, and editable instance-level assets while preserving consistent global terrain structure.
AI.conclusion: WorldClaw successfully addresses the challenge of generating large-scale, freely explorable 3D worlds from text by combining agentic planning, coarse-to-fine construction, and preservation of editable assets for downstream use.

title: Posture and Sustainment Optimization Under Adversarial Uncertainty
summary: Pre-commitment posture, the assignment of military assets to theater locations before conflict scenarios resolve, is a critical and formally unsolved problem in joint operational planning. Current practice relies on greedy heuristics that maximize value and ignore geographic coverage and are structurally vulnerable to adversaries that target high-strategic value locations. This paper presents a scenario-weighted adversarially robust posture optimization engine for the Posture and sustainability allocation (PSA) problem, modeled as a finite-horizon Markov Decision Process over assets, theater locations, and time steps. We introduce the Composite Expected Value (CEV) optimizer, which places assets by maximizing scenario-weighted expected posture efficiency over a distribution of threat scenarios, and the RobustCEV extension, which iterates against a Bayesian adversary that updates its targeting distribution in response to observed placement. Across three experiments in an Indo-Pacific basing environment with 20 assets and 5 theater locations, we demonstrate that: (1) the greedy baseline incurs a permanent 25.1% posture efficiency penalty due to geographic under-coverage and a 57.3% scenario-weighted readiness collapse under value-correlated adversarial threat; (2) the CEV optimizer recovers up to 19.8% efficiency over greedy when the threat distribution carries a geographic signal, with a curated set of 5 to 20 scenarios sufficient to capture the majority of this gain; and (3) the RobustCEV extension recovers up to 158% efficiency relative to a naive optimizer when an adaptive adversary employs a deceptive threat prior. All findings are validated using paired t-tests with Bonferroni correction and two-level variance decomposition, confirming that the performance gaps reported are structural properties of placement strategies rather than sampling artifacts.

AI.tldr: This paper presents RobustCEV, a scenario-weighted adversarial posture optimization engine that improves military asset placement by considering geographic coverage and adaptive adversaries, outperforming greedy baselines in Indo-Pacific basing scenarios.
AI.motivation: Current military posture planning uses greedy heuristics that maximize value but ignore geographic coverage, making them vulnerable to adversaries targeting high-value locations. There's a need for robust optimization that considers threat scenarios and adaptive adversaries.
AI.method: Models the Posture and sustainability allocation (PSA) problem as a finite-horizon Markov Decision Process over assets, locations, and time. Introduces Composite Expected Value (CEV) optimizer maximizing scenario-weighted expected posture efficiency, and RobustCEV extension that iterates against a Bayesian adversary updating its targeting distribution.
AI.result: In Indo-Pacific basing experiments: (1) greedy baseline incurs 25.1% efficiency penalty from geographic under-coverage and 57.3% readiness collapse under adversarial threat; (2) CEV recovers up to 19.8% efficiency over greedy with geographic threat signals; (3) RobustCEV recovers up to 158% efficiency against adaptive adversaries using deceptive threat priors.
AI.conclusion: The scenario-weighted adversarial optimization approach significantly outperforms current greedy methods for military posture planning, demonstrating the importance of considering geographic coverage, threat distributions, and adaptive adversaries. RobustCEV provides practical improvements validated with statistical significance.

title: Why the Third Axis Is Freedom
comment: Experiment code available on GitHub, in the papers folder: https://github.com/ViscousLemming/Technical-Appendices
summary: In generative training, a model produces an output and is penalised for its difference from an example. With one output per comparison, a model that produces one common answer can outperform a model retaining a broader repertoire. Explorative Modeling (XM) produces $K$ outputs per comparison and updates on the closest, claiming exploration as a "third pretraining axis" associated with generative expressivity. Here I show the third axis is actually freedom, meaning the weakness of the constraint implied by a model's behaviour. Previous work showed freedom is a property of function rather than form. Parameters, architecture, minimum-description-length (MDL), and data can vary while the behavioural constraint remains unchanged. It was formally proved that weakest models are likeliest to generalise, and freedom selection beat MDL by 110-500\% in induction experiments. I prove average XM loss depends on the chance a candidate misses an acceptable region, with exploration raising miss probability to power $K$. For $K>1$, match probability rises with freedom. I then demonstrate empirically that XM optimises for freedom. In a Forward XM experiment, larger $K$ increased or saturated measured freedom, and increased freedom at every tested value under context-dependent targets. I trained XM candidate pools and compared validation selection with a freedom selector that read unlabelled parent contexts. Freedom won in 29 of 30 cases. Generative expressivity is a mode-count proxy for freedom, that discards the extension structure that gives freedom its generalisation significance. XM is a means, freedom an end, and selecting for freedom improved XM under distribution shift.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that the "third pretraining axis" in Explorative Modeling (XM) is actually model freedom (weakness of behavioral constraints), not exploration, and shows that selecting for freedom improves generalization better than other methods.
AI.motivation: Traditional generative training penalizes model outputs compared to single examples, which can favor models that produce common answers over those retaining broader repertoires. Explorative Modeling (XM) was proposed as exploring a "third pretraining axis" for generative expressivity, but the author argues this axis is actually model freedom.
AI.method: The paper proves that average XM loss depends on the probability that a candidate model misses an acceptable region, with exploration raising this miss probability to power K. For K>1, match probability rises with freedom. Empirical demonstration includes Forward XM experiments measuring freedom with different K values, and training XM candidate pools compared against a freedom selector using unlabelled parent contexts.
AI.result: Larger K in Forward XM increased or saturated measured freedom, and increased freedom at every tested value under context-dependent targets. When comparing validation selection with freedom selection, freedom won in 29 of 30 cases. Selecting for freedom improved XM performance under distribution shift.
AI.conclusion: Generative expressivity is actually a proxy for model freedom, but discards the extension structure that gives freedom its generalization significance. XM is merely a means to achieve the end goal of increased model freedom, which is what actually drives better generalization performance.

title: OrchestraBench: Evaluating Multi-Agent Orchestration Failure Modes, Recovery, and Decomposition Quality
summary: Multi-agent orchestration frameworks are moving from demos to production, yet benchmarks typically report task accuracy without diagnosing why a pipeline failed, where a cascade began, or which routing decision caused the breakdown. OrchestraBench evaluates failure, recovery, and decomposition through a controlled, seed-reproducible failure-injection harness over templated enterprise workflows. It introduces cascade radius and per-failure-mode recovery as primary metrics and compares routing policies with bootstrap confidence intervals and paired tests. On a 26-case gold-labelled diagnostic, a keyword/flag router scored 0% on adversarial cases with misleading or missing surface flags, whereas an intent-reasoning model router scored 100%, matching the oracle. Controlled mechanism probes with a real Claude agent over a verifiable arithmetic dependency chain revealed three failure-handling tiers across five MAST modes: tool faults recovered fully (1.0), ambiguous delegation recovered partially (0.30), and three latent or semantic modes never recovered (0.0). This ordering persisted when the computation was reframed as a loan-approval workflow and across Sonnet, Opus, and Haiku, although absolute rates shifted with context. Blind retry reproduced latent faults and increased time to detection, indicating that detection and attribution are necessary for containment. Cascade radius increased with pipeline depth (mean 0.9 to 4.7 across depths 3-7). A trusted-state repair ablation showed that apparent containment gains primarily came from the trusted-state signal rather than autonomous detection. These results are controlled-chain mechanism probes, not domain-workload claims.

AI.tldr: OrchestraBench introduces a failure-injection benchmark for multi-agent systems that evaluates failure detection, recovery, and cascade containment with novel metrics like cascade radius and per-failure-mode recovery rates.
AI.motivation: Current benchmarks for multi-agent orchestration frameworks only report task accuracy without diagnosing why pipelines fail, where cascades begin, or which routing decisions cause breakdowns. There's a need for systematic evaluation of failure handling in production multi-agent systems.
AI.method: Uses a controlled, seed-reproducible failure-injection harness over templated enterprise workflows. Introduces cascade radius and per-failure-mode recovery as primary metrics. Compares routing policies with bootstrap confidence intervals and paired tests. Tests on 26-case gold-labelled diagnostics and uses controlled mechanism probes with real Claude agent over verifiable arithmetic dependency chains.
AI.result: Keyword/flag routers scored 0% on adversarial cases while intent-reasoning model routers scored 100%. Identified three failure-handling tiers: tool faults recover fully (1.0), ambiguous delegation recovers partially (0.30), and latent/semantic modes never recover (0.0). Cascade radius increased with pipeline depth (0.9 to 4.7 across depths 3-7). Blind retry reproduced latent faults and increased detection time. Trusted-state repair showed containment gains came from trusted-state signals rather than autonomous detection.
AI.conclusion: Failure detection and attribution are necessary for cascade containment in multi-agent systems. Intent-reasoning routers outperform surface-flag based routers. Different failure modes have fundamentally different recovery potentials, and system design should account for these differences. The benchmark provides systematic evaluation tools for multi-agent failure handling.

title: EvoHarness-RL: Learning Self-Evolving Runtime Harness for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
summary: Long-horizon LLM agents increasingly rely on external execution support to maintain state, track progress, invoke tools, verify outcomes, and reuse experience across interactions. However, effective harness use raises two coupled challenges: state formation from noisy interaction traces and runtime control over external-state access. Existing agents usually handle both through prompts, heuristics, or domain-specific conventions, leaving the external workspace and its usage policy manually engineered. To address this, we study the problem of harness policy learning, where agents learn harness policies offline and deploy them to construct and update external harness state online during runtime task execution. We introduce EvoHarness-RL, which exposes Belief, Progress, and Experience (BPE) as policy-facing harness state. Supervised harness fine-tuning teaches the base agent the harness action space and how to construct useful external state, while cost-aware GRPO explores coordination policies to selectively read, update, and consolidate that state during long-horizon interaction. Instantiated on ALFWorld with a Qwen3-8B LLM, EvoHarness-RL reaches 96.9% success and reveals two key dynamics: harness annealing, where training internalizes recurring harness-use patterns into the model policy and shifts the agent from frequent harness calls toward selective external-state access, and harness evolution, where progress updates and experience consolidation refine the harness into a compact, task-adaptive state substrate. These results suggest that long-horizon agents benefit from trainable policies for constructing and coordinating with external harness workspaces, beyond simply adding stronger tools or larger memories.

AI.tldr: EvoHarness-RL enables LLM agents to learn policies for constructing and coordinating with external execution harnesses, improving long-horizon task performance through selective state management rather than just adding more tools/memory.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon LLM agents rely on external execution harnesses but face two challenges: forming state from noisy interaction traces and controlling runtime access to external state. Current approaches use manual engineering via prompts/heuristics rather than learned policies.
AI.method: EvoHarness-RL introduces harness policy learning with BPE (Belief, Progress, Experience) state. Combines supervised harness fine-tuning to teach harness action space/state construction with cost-aware GRPO to explore coordination policies for selective state management during runtime.
AI.result: On ALFWorld with Qwen3-8B, achieves 96.9% success rate. Reveals harness annealing (internalizing patterns, shifting from frequent calls to selective access) and harness evolution (progress updates refining harness into compact, task-adaptive state substrate).
AI.conclusion: Long-horizon agents benefit from trainable policies for constructing and coordinating with external harness workspaces, going beyond simply adding stronger tools or larger memories. Harness policy learning enables more effective external state management.

title: Agentic self-driving microscopy benchmarks support qualification but do not necessarily generalize to unseen tasks
summary: Large language model agents are increasingly being developed to control a wide range of scientific characterization tools including microscopes and synchrotron beamlines. Research into agentic control of physical infrastructure is nascent and there are few well-established paradigms for how to engineer an agentic system. There are many choices to make when designing a microscopy agent, including the choice of LLM, the number of agents to use, agent responsibilities and delegation rules, retrieval-augmented generation parameters, and more. When designing and optimizing an agentic microscope controller, researchers not only want to ensure that the agent can correctly perform known tasks but also that the agent can generalize to new tasks that it has not encountered before. In this study, we develop a benchmark and trace-logging framework that reveals a) how different choices of agent architecture impact performance at microscopy tasks and b) the limitations of benchmarks for predicting if a particular agent will perform well on unseen microscopy tasks. The framework was used to evaluate one-, two-, and three-agent graph topologies, five LLMs, RAG and context parameters, and operational constraints across 53 microscopy benchmark tests. In total, 105 agent configurations, 1,949 individual test runs, and 49,109 RAG retrievals were recorded. Direct comparisons showed clear differences in latency, token use, cost, and failure mode between configurations. However, surrogate models trained on agent architecture and test results did not reliably predict an agent's performance on new, unseen tasks. These results show that these benchmarks are useful for qualification, regression testing, diagnosis, and direct comparison, but the current heterogeneous test suite does not support a task-independent global configuration model.

AI.tldr: Researchers developed a benchmarking framework to evaluate LLM agent architectures for controlling microscopy equipment, finding that while benchmarks help compare configurations, they don't reliably predict performance on unseen tasks.
AI.motivation: As LLM agents are increasingly used to control scientific characterization tools like microscopes, there's a need for systematic evaluation methods to understand how different agent design choices affect performance and generalization to new tasks.
AI.method: Created a benchmark and trace-logging framework to evaluate agent architectures across 53 microscopy tasks, testing one-, two-, and three-agent graph topologies, five different LLMs, RAG parameters, and operational constraints across 105 configurations and 1,949 test runs.
AI.result: Benchmarks revealed clear differences between configurations in latency, token use, cost, and failure modes, but surrogate models trained on architecture and test results failed to reliably predict performance on unseen microscopy tasks.
AI.conclusion: The developed benchmarks are useful for qualification, regression testing, and comparison of agent configurations, but current heterogeneous test suites cannot support task-independent global configuration models for predicting generalization to unseen tasks.

title: Hybrid Probabilistic Zonotopes for Identifiable and Refinable Predictive Uncertainty
summary: Probabilistic prediction heads in neural networks typically output either a Gaussian mixture or a single conformal region. Neither separates the distinct sources of uncertainty often present in real prediction tasks: a discrete choice among modes, bounded systematic drift within the chosen mode, and irreducible stochastic noise. We introduce the Hybrid Probabilistic Zonotope (HProbZ), an output head that represents these three sources as binary, bounded, and stochastic generators of a zonotope, and admits a closed-form likelihood by convolution. Sharing the bounded generator across prediction steps couples future predictions algebraically, so observing one step refines the predictive distribution at every remaining step in a single forward pass. We establish that the three generators are identifiable from the likelihood up to permutation, and that an HProbZ density is representationally distinct from any finite Gaussian mixture. The same shared structure provides analytic per-mode risk and distribution-free multi-modal conformal sets at inference time. Empirical analysis on representative prediction benchmarks supports the effectiveness of the design relative to same-encoder mixture baselines, while offering structural properties that mixture or convex-conformal predictors do not jointly provide.

AI.tldr: HProbZ is a novel neural network output head that separates prediction uncertainty into three identifiable sources (discrete mode choice, systematic drift, and noise) using zonotopes with closed-form likelihood and shared structure for multi-step refinement.
AI.motivation: Existing probabilistic prediction heads (Gaussian mixtures or single conformal regions) fail to separate the distinct sources of uncertainty present in real prediction tasks: discrete mode choices, bounded systematic drift within modes, and irreducible stochastic noise.
AI.method: Introduces Hybrid Probabilistic Zonotope (HProbZ) output head that represents three uncertainty sources as binary (mode choice), bounded (systematic drift), and stochastic (noise) generators of a zonotope. Uses shared bounded generator across prediction steps to algebraically couple future predictions, allowing single-step observations to refine all remaining predictions in one forward pass.
AI.result: Establishes that the three generators are identifiable from likelihood up to permutation, and HProbZ densities are representationally distinct from finite Gaussian mixtures. Provides analytic per-mode risk and distribution-free multi-modal conformal sets at inference. Empirical benchmarks show effectiveness over same-encoder mixture baselines.
AI.conclusion: HProbZ offers a novel probabilistic prediction framework that cleanly separates uncertainty sources, provides closed-form likelihood, enables multi-step refinement through shared structure, and offers unique capabilities not jointly available in mixture or convex-conformal predictors.

title: CASCADE: An Agentic Regulatory Network Framework for Patient-Data-Validated Downstream Perturbation Prediction
summary:
CASCADE is an agentic framework that predicts downstream transcriptional effects of gene perturbation from precomputed
  ARACNe regulatory networks, exposed via MCP. Prior work validates such tools by checking whether predicted genes are
  known cancer genes (membership); we instead test whether the predicted direction of change matches reality, using
  focal-gene copy-number amplification as a dosage-based proxy for the inverse of knockdown against real TCGA patient
  tumor data.
  For MYC, CASCADE's predicted knockdown targets show strong concordance with real amplified-vs-non-amplified tumor
  expression across three cancer types (BRCA: 90.0%, COAD: 72.0%, STAD: 85.7%; all p<0.0013), well above permutation
  baselines, surviving a PAM50 subtype control and replicating in an independent cohort (METABRIC, 87.2%). Compared
  against curated MSigDB gene-set baselines via Fisher's exact test, CASCADE's accuracy is not shown to exceed existing
  public knowledge of MYC- or E2F-driven biology, though its gene-specific direction-calling clearly outperforms a naive
  uniform guess.
  Extending to fifteen additional genes, validation proves gene-specific rather than universal: proliferation-machinery
  regulators mostly replicate, while lineage-identity transcription factors and one cyclin-D paralog (CCND2)
  consistently fail, a pattern we discuss as a hedged, post-hoc hypothesis.
  We separately benchmark whether an LLM-based agent correctly grounds natural-language requests into CASCADE's real MCP
  tool calls. Across 35 queries, a documented local model reaches 71.4% exact match (85.7% for a larger model); schema
  and gene-alias failures are resolved by scale or server-side correction, but both models confidently default to the
  wrong perturbation type on ambiguous queries, a failure a targeted fix could not resolve because its trigger condition
  never occurs.

AI.tldr: CASCADE is an agentic framework that predicts downstream transcriptional effects of gene perturbations using ARACNe networks, validated by comparing predicted direction of expression changes against real patient data using copy-number amplification as a dosage-based proxy for knockdown.
AI.motivation: Prior validation methods for gene perturbation prediction tools only check if predicted genes are known cancer genes (membership), but this doesn't test whether the predicted direction of change matches reality. The authors want to validate if predicted directionality aligns with actual expression changes in patient data.
AI.method: 1. Uses focal-gene copy-number amplification as a dosage-based proxy for the inverse of knockdown against TCGA patient tumor data. 2. Tests CASCADE's predictions by comparing whether predicted direction of expression change matches actual expression differences between amplified vs non-amplified tumors. 3. Validates across three cancer types (BRCA, COAD, STAD) and replicates in independent cohort (METABRIC). 4. Benchmarks against curated MSigDB gene-sets and permutation baselines. 5. Extends validation to fifteen additional genes. 6. Separately evaluates LLM-based agent's ability to correctly ground natural-language requests into CASCADE's MCP tool calls.
AI.result: For MYC: CASCADE's predicted knockdown targets show strong concordance with amplified-vs-non-amplified tumor expression (BRCA: 90.0%, COAD: 72.0%, STAD: 85.7%; all p<0.0013), well above permutation baselines, surviving PAM50 subtype control and replicating in METABRIC cohort (87.2%). For other genes: Validation is gene-specific - proliferation-machinery regulators mostly replicate, while lineage-identity transcription factors and CCND2 consistently fail. LLM benchmarking: Local model reaches 71.4% exact match on tool calls (85.7% for larger model), but models confidently default to wrong perturbation type on ambiguous queries.
AI.conclusion: CASCADE successfully predicts direction of expression changes for specific genes like MYC using real patient data, but validation success is gene-dependent. The framework works well for proliferation regulators but fails for lineage-identity factors, suggesting biological context matters. LLM agents can ground natural language to tool calls with moderate accuracy, but systematic issues remain with ambiguous queries that current fixes can't resolve.

title: Matrix Zonotopic Attention: A Context-Adaptive Value Projection for Set Transformers
summary: Multi-head attention combines an input-dependent softmax routing with an input-independent linear value projection, so the per-sample operator mapping aggregated values to outputs is the same for every input set. We study the consequences of this asymmetry for permutation-invariant set targets.
